forget it agalrst our friend. I wonder what they will do to them all? It will be a terrible problem for the King, the Home Secretary, the House of Lords, the whole Bench of Judges—and everybody else."
He was interrupted by a policeman, who flashed his lantern on him.

" Good evening, sir," he said, perceiving a white tie and patent boots. "Been looking at the place where poor old ' Mornv ' was killed? We get llts still coming to loo." Ben Nevis nodded. "Morbid, isn't it ? "he said.

"Yes, sir," replied the man cheerfully. 'Orriblo affair 'aftogether, as had as jack the Ripper' was. One comfort about this job is that you seem to 'ave to be a blooming lord or a Cabinet Minister to qualify, so the likes of us is safe, anyhow." Ben gave a rather 11•7,1 low laugh. "I hope so, -Robert," he remarked, think- ing of his narrow escape. "But whom do you think did it?"

" It's all right, sir," answered the police- man, with a confidential smile. "We all knows in the force. The people think us fools.; but we're only waiting our time to cop 'the lot, I give you my word. They're anarchists, sir; and they 'ang out in Soho. Old Verschoyle's got his peepers on them." "I'm gla?1 to hear said 11;n, too anxious to be amusod at the constable's confidences, , but giving him half-a-crown as he moved on.

" Now I wonder if he's the bloke as did it ?" said the policeman, seized with a sudden bright idea. "Criminals 'as a knack of coining back to the scenes of their crimes: and Lim did somehow seem to have a peculiar 'ankering after this 'ere un'oly spot. Never mind, I seed 'is face clearly and shan't forget 'im in a 'urry." . _

And the suspicious constible, with his f9ot on the first rung of the detective ladder, spat solemnly on Ben's half-crown and transferred it to his trouser pock.?:. "Not a bad bloke neither," he reflected charitably..

Ben Nevis, meanwhile, unconscious of the suspicions he had aroused in the policeman's breast, continued his way down Park Lane in an abstracted mood, arguing and re-arguing the question of his position with himself, despite the fact that he had already made up his mind definitely and clearly as to his course of action.

He baned into Piccadilly, making for Half Moon Street, when. he had rooms on the ground floor of an old-fashionecl house, kept by an old soldier and Ids wife. ' Half -Moon Street appeared quite empty, as was to be expected between half past two and three on a freezing February morning; and Ben quickened his pace, as he drew near to his diggings. On the 'steps he paused to unbutton his heavy coat and get out his latch-key, Suddenly he heard a slight sound behind him, but before he could turn he felt a sudden violent blow in the back which made bun turn sick. He fell forward, and all was black. •

div.head: THE. . .
div.p: THE. . .
WHITE ROSE.
By GERALD BISS.
CHAPTER XXIV. IN an instant they were both off the car. It was the opportunity Ben had been looking for.

As Branksea lifted the bonnet, and put his head into the engine. Ben, without a word. quietly crossed the footpath on tiptoe and plunged into a clump of trees. "Come here, Ben Nevis," call.td out the other, "and see for yourself." There was no answer, and Branksea, with- drawing his head from the engine, looked round to see where Ben Nevis was. Nowhere coulel he see a sign of his quarry, and a cold chill struck his heart. "Great God," he muttered, a look of horror crossing his evil face; "be must have smelt a rat and bolted ! Whatever shall .1 do ? "

And the foiled murderer ground his teeth with rage and chagrin. Meanwhile Ben was running swiftly across the Heath towards Frognal, determined to pit a good distance between Branksea and himself. He laughed- to himself for an instant at the thought of his abrupt departure, and the other's surprise and disgtist. Then he muttered to himself: "Oh. my God, what a foul trick. I see it now : but a motor can't farm me across country. If I hadn't noticed his buttonhole I sbould have been stuck like a pig by now, and as dead as Oddingly or Mornington or Poole or Duvall But I ought to have known ; I ought to have guessed at once. The .very fact of Lord and Lady Swanage being there owdit to have been enouTh. It would net have been safe to leave me alive ; but I've fooled them, and they shall pay for it. What • a list! - And what a plot ! It:s the biggest sensation of the age. I must see Sir Hugo Verschoyle the first thing in the mornio4."

_ Then an idea struck him—final Bina's father and mother! Whatever should he do —or could he do ? The lightness and elasticity went out of his step in an instant, and lus head sank on his chest. "What shall I do ? " he murmured, almost wildly. "My poor, poor darling,. my Bina ; what shall 1(10 ? .2dy brain is on fire : I Must think. What would she have me do, as a soldier—a man of honour? I must think; I want to think." Unconsciously he plagiarised Sir Henry Morning ton, when he had to face the same. situation. He wandered on and on, regardless of where he was' of whither he ivas ig„ trying to think, yet incapable of it. lie was like a man stunned by a blow between the eyes, coming to but still unable to control his move- ments or his senses. He tripped over a root and fell full length on the ground. The fall aroused him, and he pulled himself together by an almighty effort •sf will. He realised that he must fa... leave the Heath and get back to the West End ; and he

decided to alk. A walk would do him good, and help him to collect his thoughts and map out a plan of action. It was beginning to come home to him that, even if .he had lost Bina for ever and the light went out of his life, he had no alternative but to make a clean breast of the whole thing to Sir Hugo Ver- schoyle, and place the information in his hands. But it was hard to bb put into such a quandary and to have the cup of happiness snatched from his thirsty lips through no fault of his own. Yet he had learnt the lesson of duty before he had learut to love; but love without 'honour was a sorry alternative. to nonour without love. Then came the remembrance of his meeting with Bina in the Park at noon to-morrow—

no, that day. He looked at his watch and found that it was lion," after one o'clock. What should he do; what should he say to her? Anyhow, he would have seen Sir Hugo before that, and perhaps—perhaps Sir Hugo might take immediate action— even arrest the Duke and Duchess of Hamp- stead, and then he might never see Bina again. . _
But what if his story were laughed at? What if they refused to take it seriously and put him down as a crank? Then he would lose Bina without any good being done by the

sacrifice. On the faCe -of it it looked absurd; and in cold blood, in black and white, it would seem hideously ridiculous. But for all thot, it was none the less true, none the less hor- rible; and he at least knew that he had not been dreaming or imagining vain things. He only wished devoutly that he had.

At last he found hirilself off the Heath, in Frognal. a district he did not know at all; but he struck out a line for himself to the south- west, judging by general direction, and walked quickly on: torn between love and honour—as many a good man before him. Soon he struck the Finchley road and recognised it as a main thoroughfare. By then he felt himself safe .from pursuit, and his . . .

only idea was to walk his brain clear, if he could, and to arrange a plan of campaign. • As he walked on' down the winding North Read the inevitability of his course of action' grew upon him, and he felt that he could neither hesitate nor attempt to compromise for private reasons. That would make him an accomplice to the murders. He must face the future, and, in a/1 probability, bid adieu to love for good and all. A few hours before all had seemed so bright, and now there was nothing but blackness ahead. It would be an awful blow for Bina, in the heyday of her youth mid beauty. From . .
being the most cOurted and the mOst envied girl in Great Britain she would fall in an in- stant from her pinnacle to the heritage of a dis-
honoured name ; and that blow mu-st, by the
decree of fate, be dealt by his hand. All his great love would not allow him to soften it one iota.

In his agony of mind he could have cried out aloud in the middle of the street, but lie re- strained himself from habit and sheer despair. How would Bina takes In the selfishness of love Belsize hardly entered into his thoughts and calculations. Proudly, he was certain, and with a stiff upper lip ; but it would break her heart. She would never look .him in the face again. It was beyond human power to forgive such a blow and, however illogical it might be, to love in the same way the man who had dealt it. For an instant he even contemplated suicide, suicide without a word of explana- tion, for her sake: and the idea seemed sweet in its self-sacrifice. But only for an instant; then he realised that it would be purely selfish, after all—a• coward's way out of a hole. It would only deal her a still More deadly blow without in any way warding off the inevitable discovery. What fools these puny plotters were to think that they could pit their petty power and little wits against the strength of an established monarchy ! It was the old parable of the mustard seed ; it was a vain tizlea which had grown surprisingly and got out of hand. Besides, such a step would also make hirri a moral accomplice after the act. No, it had got to be faced in all its blackness, and he felt, with a shade of cowardice, that he was almost sorry that he had prevented Branksea's hand from solving for him the problem which was racking his brain and his heart.

Down through St. John's Wood he walked, hardly looking where he was going, and straight on through Gloucester Place, .crossing Portman Square and Oxford Street. Then he recognised where he was, and kept straight on down Park Street.
An unaccountable morbid fascination made him turn to the right at Mount Street, and crew him irresistibly to the spot where Sit Harry Mornington had been murdered.

There he paused for a moment. " I wonder which of them did it? " he murmured to himself. " Perhaps that black- jowled brute llranksea is murderer-in-chief to the gang. Anyhow, if he had had his way, I should have been dead mutton by now—as dead as poor old Mornington ! It's not his fault, and I'm lucky in some ways to have escaned t••• :•• ,--,ere premonition: but I shan't

div.head: CHAPTER XXV.
div.p: CHAPTER XXV.

THE following morning Bina, with her accustomed decision of character, plunged straight into the business of the day by storming her mother's sanctum and bearding her parents in their den. She found them talking together in low anxious tones, which ceased at her entry. "Good morning, mother; good morning, father," she said, as she kissed them: "You neither of you look as though you had slept • well. What's worrying you both? " Conscious of the terrible tragedy hanging over her head, and the part they were forced to play in it, neither spoke for a moment ; but her mother returned her kiss with unusual tenderness, which the girl took as a favour- able omen.
At last the duke spoke. "This affair of yours, dear, is causing your mother and myself a lot of anxiety. We wish you would come to our way of thinking." The duchess nodded.

" But, father dear, I love him 'very dearly," the girl answered, blushing at the self-con- sciousness of an open avowal, "very, very dearly, indeed : and there is nothing against him. Apart from money, of which we all of us have plenty and to spare, he is an excellent match."

Her father ignored the point. "You hardly know the man," he asserted, as though to force conviction on hinis,3lf. "It's only a clay or two since you met him, and you can't really care much for him. It's a fancy that will pass." "I know I have not known him long," agreed Bina, conceding his first point, "but it doesn't take one long to learn of love. And I have seen a lot of him since we met ; and I seem to have known him all my life. In fact, I don't think I was really alive till I knew him." she concluded with a soft, happy laugh. The duchess still kept silence, playing with her rings, with a frown on her forehead.

, " Faugh," exclaimed the duke, giving way to the irritation of his strained feelings, ' you talk like an under-housemaid. What's more, it's hardly decent. You should learn to control yourself and your feelings better, Sabina it is only due to your position." "Father," she interrupted, colouring hotly, "how dare you speak to me like this? won't stand it."

The duke shrugged his shoulders and kicked viciously at the hearth-rug. Obvious- ly, he was in a very bad temper. " Shush, dear," said the duc„hess, speaking for the first time, " don't let us quarrel. You know, Bina, how dearly we both love you, and how proud we are of you. That is why we do not wish to see you throw yourself away on a pauper earl, when you have the whole world at your feet." Bina listened in silence. Then she spoke more gently. "But, mother dear, I don't want the whole world. I want Ben."

" The Earl of Ben Nevis," said the duke, laying stress on his full name, " is by now per- fectly well aware that we will not entertain has proposal for your hand ; and if he is a man of any proper pride or self-respect he will at once withdraw all pretensions." Bina laughed scornfully.

"You forget," she said decidedly. "that I have a voice in the matter, and am not absolutely a cypher. Ben won the V.C. in South Africa, and is hardly likely to be afraid of pompous parents—especially with me to back him." Then she grew more gentle. "But, father, don't let us be angry with each orner : We've always been such good friends hitherto. You must see that I'm determined —determined to be happy. It's more to me than to anyone else ; and I can be obstinate, too, if necessary." Her father, obviously in a quandarf, was fuming. Her mother was white and looked twenty years older than the day before. They both felt that they were playing a terribly tragic farce. "You would get over it in a month," said.. the duke sophistically, as much to appease his own coriscience as his daughter; "and, as I have said, I will not have you throw away your brllliant prospects—the most brilliant in the whole Empire. We have other views, other hopes for you, our only daughter." " It's my belief that you want me to marry your mysterious Mr. • Stuart," retorted the girl scornfully. "I believe he is some big foreign grandee in disguise, or a petty princeling with an eye on the family plate." Her parents both started almost imper- ceptibly. Whatever you choose to think," answered the duke, snappishly, "will not alter our decision with regard to Lord Ben Nevis; so you may take it as final." Bina moved towards the door without another word. As she opened it she paused and spoke in a strained voice. "Then the conduct of the affair is left in my hands. Remember, my parole has expired!' The door closed behind her before either af her parents could speak. " Poor, poor child," exclaimed her mother In a half-strangled voice," "it will break her heart when she hears. But it would have been more cruel to pretend to give way under the circ..rratnlces ; it will give her oride

By five and twenty minutes past her share ort be 13:Isize ternper began to assert itself, and :shc became piqued and annoyed. No man had ever kept her waiting before; and consistent flattery had . tended to make her unconsciously imp .rious. " I'll give him till the half-hour," she murmured with e -aordinary generosity, pursing her lips ; "if le doesn't turn up by then I shall go home. Perhaps there'll be a wire or a message," ,she thought a little forlornly: - But the maiden all forlorn had never been Bina's role in life ; and as the long hand passed the rubicon, up she jumped, calling Mike a little sharply to heel. He trotted beside her, panting disgustedly and feeling that there was something wrong with the world, as no notice had beeen taken of his repeated, overtures. His mistri:si walked quickly towards Hyde Park Corner, disgusted with the result of her first love-tryst: Maidens arc very exacting in the early days of courtship, yet full of excuse for everything in their lovers except neglect. Her reflections were interrupted by the sound of raucous shouts borne on the breeze. It brought back to her her walk in• the park with Ben. div.head: ST. JAMES' BAZAAR.
div.p: ST. JAMES' BAZAAR.
Gratifying Result. i

The result of the bazaar held in St. James' school on Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday last more than realized the most sanguine expectations of the promoters, tie sum raised being £595. It was announced that the amount would be. increased te £6OO daring the week. On Saturday after- noon the bazaar was opened by Mrs. Powell, of Sewerby Vicarage, Bridlington, in the presence of a large gathering. The Vicar presided and said he had no need to introduce Mrs. Powell who was well-known to the people of the parish. One of the objects of the bazaar which would no doubt be of special interest to Mrs. Powell was the extinguishing of the debt on St. Hilda's Mission. That institution was inaugurated during Mr. Powell's incumbency and in his (the speaker's) opinion that was one of the wisest steps ever taken in connection with the parish. The mission was doing well, the congregations were increasing, a club for young men was in daily use, and the building served a very useful purpose indeed. He was sorry that Mr. Powell could not be with them as he_was detained by a lecturing engagement. Mrs. Powell con'veyed her husband's kind regards to the parishioner; and expressed his great regret that he could not be present. She was very pleased to be able to come among them again. When she said she was sorry to leave Warrington she did not think people quite believed her, but thought she was trying to be polite. She was, however, more sorry to leave the town than she could express. She was glad to see how pros- perous and happy they seemed to be and that they were all pulling together for the good of St. James's. She was particularly glad to hear that the bazaar was being conducted without any raffles. Some of them would remember the vigorous crusade which her husband waged a few years ago against ;a:Wiling, and he was very pleased that there were to be no raffles at that bazaar. She heard it had made very little difference to the pro- ceeds. Some of the larger things would perhaps be left on their hands, but they could be kept to form the basis of another bazaar. They would always have the satisfaction of knowing that they had kept the standard high. (Applause.) A lovely bouquet was presented to Mrs. Powell by Miss Gladys Hackney. On the motion of Mr. H. N. HocouToN, seconded by Mr. J. ECeCERSLEY, a hearty vete of thanks was accorded to Mrs. Powell, and the business of the day commenced.

BRUTAL ASSAULT. At Runcorn, on Monday, John Igo, a loafer with a bad record, for assaulting James Hambleton, a crippled shrimper and stealing food and a cap, was sentenced to three months' hard labour. Igo took charge of Haruble- ton's boat, and beat Lim insensible with a piece of iron piping.

div.head: LIGHTNING "FLICKER."
div.p: THE LIGHTNING "FLICKER."

The " flicker " sometimes noticed in lightning proves to be due to the fact that several flashes —sometimes five or six—follow one path too rapidly to be separated by the eye. The trails shown in, photography of very bright Rashes are caused by incandescence produced in the air for a very brief period. ,

RONTGEN RAYS USEFUL. A novel use of Röntgen rays is made by a Berlin company manufacturing submarine cables. The cables are tested by being passed over two eye-pulleys over an g•-ray tube, tho screen above shewing any defect more directly and with greater certainty than the resistance tests usually employed.

div.head: 'MAGNETIC STORMS.
div.p: 'MAGNETIC STORMS.

The hypothesis that magnetic storms, auroras, dtc., are due to the passage of the earth through denser portions of matter ejected by the sun is favoured by Professor Sehaeberle, the German astronomer. He finds that the irregularity of period is what should be expected, and the phe- nomena of comets sustain this view.

div.head: CALCIUM STEEL.
div.p: CALCIUM STEEL.

A substance obtained from a mixture of fels- par, sand, and lime, and somewhat curiously called "calcium steel," promises to be of some importance in the arts. As formed from the fusion of these ingredients it is described as a compact homogeneous inass. When cooled it is of great hardness, resists oxidation, and is not affected by acids. It is also a bad conductor of heat and electricity.

div.head: SEPARATION OF TANTALUM.
div.p: SEPARATION OF TANTALUM.

According to the Mining Journal, Mr. Henry Bailey, F.C.S., has perfected a method for the ,separation of tantalum oxide from the comparatively useless niobium oxide. The dis- covery. is stated to be one of considerable impor- tance, in that it should give a commercial value to those deposits of tantalite which at present, and owing to the presence of a high percentage of niobium, remain unworked and practically useless.

div.head: THUNDERSTORM REGISTER.
div.p: A THUNDERSTORM REGISTER.

Professor A. Turpain has described to the French Physical Society an instrument for automatically registering thunderstorms. It con- sists of a series of coherers arranged in circuits. The action of the electric discharge of the at- mosphere introduces these coherers into the cir- cuit of a highly-sensitive galvanometer. The deflections of the latter are then recorded oh a moving photographic plate. Thus the intensity of the thunderstorm is automatically registered.

div.head: LUNATICS' BRAINS.
div.p: LUNATICS' BRAINS.

It is a popular idea that the heavier the brain is the higher are the intellectual possibilities of its possessor. An eminent doctor says that a heavy brain is no indication of intellectual eminence. The average weight of the European brain is from 490 z. to 500 z., yet five out of thirty-one male lunatics, taken without selection from post-mortem records, had brains ranging from 50oz. to 560 z. The brains of three female lunatics out of twenty-two exceeded 50oz. It is well known that epileptics .usually have large brains.

" BARsZCZ." • "Barszcz" is the name given in Poland to a fermentation product of beetroot. It is largely used as a food, especially in invalid diets. It is described as a viscid, thread-like fluid, of a red colour, aromatic smell, and pleasant acid sweet taste. " Barszcz" is the result of what is known as slime fermentation produced by the action of certain bacteria. To prepare it the beetroot is cleaned, cut in slices, and placed in soft water. Fermentation sets in, and in a week the process is complete. It is then filtered through linen, and is ready for use.

div.head: SUICIDE AND SEX.
div.p: SUICIDE AND SEX.

I Professor Bailel, of Yale, dealing with 29,344 cases of suicide recorded between 1897 and 1901, finds that the male suicides ' outnumber those of the "weaker sex " by seven to two, while as re- gards the age-incidence of a morbid inclination towards felo-de-se the age-period of twenty to fifty covers nearly two-thirds of all the cases. This would seem to indicate. the British Medi- cal Journal thinks, that milder the lower age- limit there are few to whom life seems unattrac- tive, while after fifty a natural end looms so near that it ia scarcely worth while to precipi. \tate its arrival.

HOW WE HEAR VOWELS. The hearing of vowels has been a subject of investigation by Dr. Marage, the French physician. He has used a "vowel siren," and has shewn that every vowel is perceived at a certain distance with a minimum of energy on some particular note, and that, in consequence, the ear hears each vowel better on some notes than on others. The e and i. need the sharp notes; ~the o and a carry the voice. The experiments seem to indicate that the present "re " emitted by the sirens of lighthouses could be changed to some other note that would carry further with less expenditure of energy.

div.head: 'QUEER VOICE COLLECTIONS.
div.p: 'QUEER VOICE COLLECTIONS.

Collections of voices are being made for vari- ous purposes. The phonogranis of the British Museum are designed to preserve for future generations the voices of famous people of our time; but the Vienna Academy of Sciences is going further, and seeks phonograms of lan- guages and dialects for the comparative study of languages. Already its collection includes popu- lar songs of gipsies and Arabians, favourite airs of Red Indian tribes, the idioms of Negroes and Malays, and so on. It is sending out special voice-hunting expeditions every year, and its agents are now scouring Australasia, Roumania, Istria, and other localities. Its latest plan is to phonograph the voices of animals, for scientific study.

PERIODICITY OF INSECT VISITATIONS. The losses occasioned by insects to farm pro- ducts exhibit a wide range in different years, due, as a rule, to favourable or unfavourable climatic conditions, and also to the abundance, from time to time, of natural enemies. The re- sult is more or leso periodicity in the occurrence of bad insect years. In other words, periods of unusual abundance of particular insect pests are, as a rule, followed by a number of years of com- parative scarcity. Furthermore, seasons which may be favourable to one insect may prove un- favourable to others, hence there may be not only periodicity in the occurrence of the same insect, but more or less of a rotation of the different insect pests of particular crops.

`. TELEGRAPHING PHOTOGRAPHS. The well-known electrical inventor Professor Korn. in a lecture at Munich before the members of the Electro-Technical Association, described the progress made towards the perfection of the apparatus for transmitting photographs Over telegraph wires. Professor Korn stated that the problem of telegraphing photographs had been solved in principle. The experiments al- ready carried out prove that it is possible to trans- mit a photograph or sketch, six or seven inches square, in a period varying from to to twenty minutes. These experiments were carried out on the telegraph line from Munich to Nuremberg, a distance of about 100 miles, but Professor Korn declares that precisely the same results would be obtained if the photographs were transmitted by a telegraph line or submarine cable 5,000 milos in length. The photogyaph which has to bo transmitted is placed on a , transparent glass cylinder, which revolves slowly, and at the same time moves from right to left. A ray of light is thrown on this cylinder by means of an electric lamp and lens, and when the ray of light reaches the in- terior of the cylinder it is brighter or darker, ac- cording to the colouring of that particular part of the photograph through which it passes. In- side the cylinder is some selenium, which trans- mits the electrical current in proportion to the intensity of light brought to bear on it. The selenium transmits the current more rapidly in a bright light, and less rapidly as the light de- creases. Tho selenium within the cylinder is connected with the wire over which the photo- graph is to be transmitted. The receiving station consists of an electrical Nernst lamp plaoed inside a glass cylinder ....evered with sensitised paper. The Nernst lamp burns more or less brightly according to the varying current • transmitted by the selenium at the other end. It thus reproduces the exact shade of the original photograph, provided that the cylinders at each end of the wire revolve at exactly the same speed. The professor has as- certained a simple means of regulating the re- volution of the cylinders so that the speed is identical at both ends.

Professor Korn stated that when the improve- ments on which he is now working are intro- duced it will be possible to transmit a photo- graph or sketch, of half-a-dozen inches andare, within fire seconds, instead of ton or fifteen mittutos.

div.head: ECZEMA IN WINTER.

Increased Prevalence of This

div.head: HOW TO MAKE THE BEST OF LIFE. ---- Address by Mr. Robert Cameron M.P.
div.p: HOW TO MAKE THE BEST OF LIFE. ---- Address by Mr. Robert Cameron M.P.

A well attended meeting of the Penketh Wesleyan Men's Bible Class was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom on Monday evening when an address on How to make the best of life " was delivered by Mr. Robert Cameron M.P. The chair was occupied by Mr. James Dodds,who• said he rejoiced to be associated with Mr. Cameron, his old and true friend, and he felt it no slight honour to preside for him on that occasion. It was about forty years ago at Newcastle that he looked upon Mr. Cameron as an incentive for his future life, and he owed more to him than to snyone else what he was to-day. (Applause). It was nine years since Mr. Cameron first came to Penketh, and he sincerely hoped that he would be spared to come there again. (Applause). Mr. Cameron said he thought his subject would be a suitable one to those who were just beginning life. Those who were declining should make the best ot the time that was left. There were scores of things which made men happier, and scores of things which made them miserable. He would Tut the question before them : " What was life? " It was a mysterious prin- ciple that gave the vegetable the power to develop and grow and it was a mysterious principle that made the heart beat and allowed the ear to hear and the hand to work. It was worth their time to study and understand these things. Their lives could be developed into nobleness, or their happiness ccruld be weakened, destroyed, and degraded. Let them study those things and try to do good throughout their lives. Happiness came out of a good home, where there were healthy, intelligent Mid pious parents—the greatest gifts they could possibly have. (Applause.) In miserable homes, people never beard of books or kindness,but they heard quarrels and saw drunkennesd. Opportunities for happiness were infinitely increasing. Let them not undervalue education, or the training that was given to them. It was very inportant as the brain should be drilled and people should understand science, and the history of the world, and its literature Let them read the best of books as the man who was ignorant was liable to all sorts of delusions. Knowledge was power and helped character, and widened their manhood. One of the most powerful influences in this life was the friendships they formed, especially when young. Let their friends be of the right sort, and choose those who were stronger, wiser, and nobler than themselves. and who would stimulate them and open the world to them (Applause). The man who could make the best of life must learn to train himself and to work for others. If a man lived for himself only, and to make money he could not be thoroughly happy. John Burns, who was full of life, made the best of the gift and faculties given to him, and he found happiness now in having helped the poor. If they would be happy they must make sacrifices for other. (Applause). During the evening Miss Constance Raton, of Salop, sweetly sang " Song oft Paradise," and " Eternal rest," which were loudly applauded.—A hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Cameron and Miss Eaton. A collec- tion was taken in aid of the chapel funds.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Warwick Pageant.--Warwick Castle is associated • with many stirring events in the history of England,and it is contemplated to make it the central figure in another historic pageant, next year, like that of Sher- borne last summer. Few places could be better chosen for such a purpose than this famous castle, which was the home of the ancient and mighty Earls of Warwick. The present Earldom is of course a re-creation of a much later date. As history relates, the last of the original Earls of Warwick fell at the battle of Barnet, in 1471. The last of the second line died childless, in 1589, and for twenty nine years there were no Earls of Warwick. A third line came into existence, bat that was also extinguished by the death of the eighth earl without heirs. The present Earl of Warwick is decend- -ed from Sir Fulke Greville, upon whom the Barony of Brooke was conferred, together with a grant of Warwick " Castle, in 1620, but the Earldom, with the right to use 'the arms of the ancient Earls of Warwick, was not revived until the year 1759. The Romance of a Famous Actress.—Grey's Cliffe,the beautiful home of Lord Agernon Percy in the near neighbourhood of Warwick Castle, is associated with a -romantic story of a very famous actress. In the year 1772 a company of strolling players came to Warwick -under a certain Roger Kemble, who had a very beautiful daughter, Sarah, then aged seventeen. She was one of the players, and to the great annoyance of her father, was deeply in love with William Siddons, another member of the company. So the father, thinking to -part them, hired Sarah as a maid to Lady Mary Greathead, of Grey's Chile. But the scheme WFLS futile, like so many others of its kind, and in the 'following year Sarah married her lover at Coventry and -afterwards became known to fame as the great" Mrs. "Siddons." The Greatheads had the highest respect for 'her, and for many years afterwards Mrs. Siddons was a

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November. 11, 1905.

Bead Necklaces.—Lovers of beads will rejoice at the advent of pink-tinged white coral ; and quartz which, colourless itself, is dyed pink in some wonderful and• mysterious way. To secure a necklace of a shade to I match one's gown, is a quite simple task, as beads may ' now be had in every colour of the rainbow. There are porcelain or glass beads, for example, imitating the opal, chysoprase, amethyst, turquoize, and amber, and so beautiful are they, that no one feels the least shame in wearing them. Many society women possessed of I the most magnificent jewellery may be seen wearing I these pretty bead necklaces, and such individuals have been heard to remark that quite as much pleasure, and very much less anxiety is attached to the wearing of them, than to strings of pektrls, diamonds, and other I priceless gems. Green Dining Rooms.—There are signs that the red I dining room is played out," it being deemed by those women who carefully study effects, less successful thaa I a green dining apartment. Undoubtedly these observant persons are correct in their views, for in the green of the leaves and trees, we have Nature's own background, with which every possible hue seems to harmonise. For setting off gowns and complexions there is nothing really to equal a green apartment, provided of course, the soft, and most becoming shades are fixed upon. The paper should be plain, or patterned in a conventional design in two or three shades of the same colour, the paint in the former instance being white, while in the I latter, a medium tone of green should be selected. The ' curtains when plain parer is chosen, should be of th same tone exactly, but when a patterned paper is pre- ferred, they should match the paint, while the carpet would look well, in each instance, it a darker shade. Curtains and PortikSres.—ln those rooms where there is much design, either on the walls or in the covering, such fabrics as plain serge, cloth or corduroy velveteen, are the best, for curtains and portieres. The plain cloth curtain, bordered with velvet, and furnished at the edge by a narrow trimming, is having a great vogue, at the momeut. Where plain walls, furniture covers, and carpet save been selected however, patteraed draperies are permissible, and in such instances the old world soft toned damasks are very much to the fore again. Then there are the fashionable wool and silk tapestries, and silk and chenille hangings, which need no lining and no triroming beyond a silk cord at the edge. All curtains and portieries it should be remembered, must fall easily and gracefully, without any pulling out of the natural line, and so suggest the appearance of having arranged themselves. .

The Perfume Craze. —The craze for sachets sewn into our gowns. wraps, headgear, and underwear, and pluced in all receptacles for wearing apparel, and also in our baths, does not end here. If we are" smart," we must perfume our apartments,the same scent being employed, of course. Many society women waft heliotrope,violet, or white rose, over their rooms by means of a syringe, others use liquid scout, which, when ignited by a match, throws around an odour that is both sweet and pene- trating, while yet again, others perfume their apartments by tilling sanoers with essences, and placing them here' there and everywhere, or spray pieces of muslin secured across the openings of the windows. wi tic their favourite scent, which causes a perfumed breeze to be wafted over the rooms. Provided we kesp all this sort of thing strictly within moderation, little can be said and the gentlewoman will not need to be told that in the matter of rooms, as in one's person, only the faintest suggestion of perfume is desirable.

Shopping Reform.—Those London shopkeepers who have dispensed with the too officious floor walker, have found this policy a great success. Many women who would like to go into a shop to look round are deterred by the thought that they will beMet on the threshold with a demand to say what they require. They want aothing in particular, but are not unlikely customers, ! they happen to see anything that takes their fancy. 'iopkeepers now see the wisdom of encouraging such -hors, and at many of the great establishments, one enter and look round the various departments with- Ong- asked any questions. Some say that this will mean increased work for the weary shop listants but this does not follow and at any rate meased trade should mean increased pay for the iistants, and employment for a larger number. DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
" VESITTIti " RED.

The new "Vesuyius" red, whose exact shade dose who are familiar with the sight of a sun- ict on the Bay of Naples will have no difficulty in determining, is seen to best advantage in woollen materials, for in silk and satin it is too " voyant." As it is one of those reds which incline to blue, rather than to yellow or brown, it hardly can be said to combine well with black, but is seen to best advantage when "toned down" with a deeper shade of its own colour, velvet in the form of trimmings giving it the requisite softness.
PRETTY DANCE FROCK.

With the approach of winter, dances and other evening entertainments are weekly becoming more numerous, and a pretty evening gown is becoming a matter of necessity. A charming and inexpensive little dance frock is ii.luitrated in our sketch. The material of which it is fashioned is a spotted net in a deep shade of cream, lined with white silk, or white batiste if strict economy must be observed. The bebe bodice is very full, and is pouched over a high swathed corselet belt of pale rose chiffon velours.

The berthe of net encircling the r7(,o77elage has an edging of the same lovely material, while it is further adorned by round pastilles of the rose velvet, arranged in a double row. The skirt is plain and very full, touching the ground all round. A three-inch band of the pink velvet and five rows of velvet pastilles in graduated sizes trim the bottom of this charming dress.

div.head: UNREMIJNERATIVE EMPLOYUENTS.
div.p: UNREMIJNERATIVE EMPLOYUENTS.

It It always more stimulating when opinions are expressed with which one is half in agree- ment than when anything is said that evokes either one's entire coneurrence or dissent. For this reason, says the Queen, we welcome a letter that we have received from a correspondent, ' signing herself "Betty," in which we are asked to draw particular attention to unsatisfactory • employments. This lady writs: I come across a large number of cases where ladies have lost money, time, and often their best chances of employment by embarking in one or other of the new, untried occupations for women which are advocated by some newspapers in search of copy, or puffed by interested persons. As an instance of what I mean, I may mention gardening. There are, no doubt, a few institu- tions which deal with inebriate, lunatic, or feeble-minded women, who will employ women gardeners, but the salaries are low, and it leads to nothing. I cannot find any woman nursery gardener who has made a profit of £lOO a- year for five consecutive years after paying all ex- penses and her own keep. Gardening is only worth taking up if one is going to live with a relation in the Colonies, or if one has a very large garden of one's own; but in both these eases the lady merely saves the salary of a skilled superintendent. She will not make any- thing much beyond paying the wages, manure, and seed bill, and will be exceedingly lucky if she does that. Bookbinding and enamelled jewellery are other occupations advocated by some. Both are interesting; hut s there is no money in them. The demand for finely-bound books is small; the . demand for enamels is a fashion which is already passin,g over. Decorat- ing and furnishing were much puffed at one time. One or two of the women decorators who started fifteen or twenty years ago still hold out; but anyone who knows the business would, I feel sure, caution any -girl against enibarking her capital in Such a business to-day. I cannot too strongly impress on women that no occupa- tion is worth taking up in which they cannot see tliea way to ensuring a competency of £6O a-year at the age of fifty-five.

div.head: DELAINE BLOUSE.
div.p: DELAINE BLOUSE.

A suggestion for making up One of the pretty Paisley-patterned delaines is shewn in our sketch. The blouse is made on a lining, and the fastening is effected behind, beneath a narrow box-pleat. On each side of the pleat there are two flat tucks, which relieve the plainness of toe back. The under-vest and collar are of cream Breton net, closely gathered. It is attached to the wad the how- of the blouse are

lightly stitched down over it. The fronts are cut out in scallops and are hemmed with a border of pale-blue taffetas. They are held to. gether with a cord of pale-blue silk, which is tied in a knot at the neck, and is crossed over in front and passed through silk-covered rings, the , cord being finished at each end with a small ' tassel. The cuffs are also shaped to match the fronts, and are bound with taffetas: and the wide, folded belt of taffetas is finished with a pretty buckle. MISS ETA BOOTH'S ILLNESS. I "Lorna" says, in the Eriti.sh Weekly, that there was no foundation for the report from New York that Miss Eve'. Booth *was suffering from appendicitis. The strain of her position as head of the Salvation Army in America is very heavy, and lately, when she was conduct- , ing important eauipaig,ns in the States, she i worked too hard even for a Booth. The result ! was a breakdown in health, but she has good recuperative powers, and is already much better. Miss Eva Booth was last in England about eighteen mouths ago for the Inter- national S.A. Congress. TO-DAY'S RECIPE. ROAST HAHNCE OF VENISON.—UnIess the ; weather is very dry and mild, a haunch of venison may be hung for a fortnight. Flour it well, and sprinkle it over with pepper. Take it down every day and wipe it quite dry. Add more flour and pepper when necessary. Wash it well Mere cooking, and dry it well with a cloth. Cover it with a sheet of buttered paper, then a flour and water paste about half-an-inch thick, and then two sheets of greased paper; tie it on firmly with strong tape. Put it down in front of a good fire. Baste it well with good dripping, and continue to baste it all the time it is cooking. Half -an • hour before it is done, remove the miner and paste, dredge the haunch with uour, and baste well with butter until it ta nicely frothed. Send it to table on a hot-water dish, and put a frill on the knuckle. Serve its own gravy in a tureen and red-currant

div.head: Warrington Lose at Runcorn.
div.p: Warrington Lose at Runcorn.

Though still represented by a weak team Warrington went to Runcorn not without hopes of getting points in the Northern League and the South West Lancashire Cup Competition. In addition to the various players suffering from injury, Harris and Boardman were also absentees. The home team was short of Houghton and Walker. A strong contingent of supporters followed the Warrington men, and in consequence the Runcorn club had the best gate of the season—one of about 3,000 people, Fine weather prevailed and the ground was in excellent order.- Teams and officials :

Runcorn—Harrison, back ; Moran, Butterworth, Hesketh, and Allan, three-quarter backs ; Jolley and Flanagan, half backs ; Richardson, Dixon, Dobson, Kennedy, Leyland, Williams, Smith and Padbury, forwards.

%Vern ngton —Hallam, back ; Knisht, Isherwood, Hewitt and Brooks, three-quarter bac‘s ; Hockenhall, and Davies, half backs ; Preston, Shugars, Thomas, Jolley, Cooke, Harmer, Swift and Belton, forwards. Referee, Mt. C. aibson, Salford. Touch judges, Messrs. H. Worm% Leigh and F. Little, St. Helens. Runcorn started operations against alight breeze, and Knight returned with interest. A penalty kick gave Warrington further advantage and Runcorn,were at once penned on their lines. Thomas broke away from a scrummage and nearly forced his way over. Warrington pressed hotly, but a bad pass by Hockenhall was intercepted by Flanagan who transferred play to the centre. Warrington continued to get possession,!but the passing was very faulty. Once Davies got cleverly away and made a nice opening, but Hewitt's pass was intercepted by Butterworth who ran nearly to the War- rington line before Hockenlaall brought him down. Strong forward work by Warrington soon tooic play to the Runcorn line again. A really smart bout of passing between Davies, Hewitt and Knight resulted in the latter rushing over only to be knocked into touch-in-goal. Runcorn were unable to get the ball away, and being penalised Preston kicked a tine goal from near touch. The bomesters responded well to this reverse, and Hockelahall was lucky to stop n rush on the line. Some keen play followed here, and Jolley dropped for goal, the ball passing under bar—a lucky escape for Warrington. Fine forcing tactics by the Warrington forwards again drove the home team back, and a series of transfers on the left wing resulted in Brooks running over at the corner,only to be whistled back. Half time Warrington I goal. Runcorn nil. The second half opened with a spell of exchange punt- ing which left play pretty well in midfield. Runcorn showed much more dash than in the opening half, the forwards putting in a tremendous lot of work. Judic- ious touch-kicking by Jolley eventually forced Warring- ' ton to their own quarter. Here Thomas went into the three-quarter line with disastrous results. Instead of commanding the ball, Warrington lost it to the Run- corn forwards who heeled out six successive runs. Eventually Jolley cross-kicked, and Brooks being out of position, Moran got an easy try at the corner amid deafening cheers from the home partizans. The fact that the visitors were now in a minority spurred them on, and fora few minutes the Runcorn men were rushed off their feet. Warrington tried passing. and Knight made a good effort hut was captured. Then a penalty to Runcorn raised the siege, and they quickly rushed the hall to the Warrington end. The same tactics ensued. Thomas left the pack'and Runcorn got the ball. Finally Jolley dropped a smart goal, and the close soon came witn ituncorn winners by 1 goal 1 try (5 points) to Warrington 1 goal (2 points).

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCH.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCH.

WARRINGTON " A " T. RUNCORN "A."—Played at Warrington on Saturday. Runcorn started and Hartley replying, the early phases of the game were fought in the huncorn quarters. Hall was nicely served by Gar- side, but failed at finishing touches. A like remark applies to an effort by Kenyon, but this plaier Came near scoring the next minute when he dribbled through the Runcorn backs. Hough, however. cleared, and the visitors showing improved flrm, Warrington had to resort to defensive tactics. Ashton relieved his lines, and the home men forced their way to the Runcorn line, Jordan scoring a try, the same player adding the extra points. Runcorn again got dangerously near as the result. of excellent combination, and the left wing was pulled up at the corner. Lloyd relieved, and Warring- ton again taking up the attack, Garside served Jordan, who promptly sent on to Kenyon, a capital try being the result. Garside added the goal, and Warrington led at the interval by ten points to nil. Turning round the leaders immediately forced the pace, and Kenyon soon augmented the score with another fine try. Hartley next crossed, followed by Shaw. Garside placed a goal, and Warrington won by three goals five tries (21points), to Runcorn nil.

The visitors, loy good forward play, worked their way into the home quarters, but W. Gibbs sent the ball back to mid-field. From a scrimmage underneath the posts, Daintith ran over, scoring his third try. Davenport added the extra points. No more scoring took place, and Stockton Heath NVOR by 11 points to nil.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

P.S.A. Society Meetings. The meeting of the Buckley-street Society which was held on Sunday was well attended. Mr. Davey-Smith presided, and gave an address choosing for his subject " Rubbish " Mr. Truman (of Liverpool) was the speaker, and based his remarks upon the words o' What ;hall I do, then, with Jesus which is called Christ ? " The soloist was Miss M. Plinstou. Mrs. Simpson and Mr. H. Woolley also took part in the service. Mr. R. NELsou (vice-president) presided over the usual weekly meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. Society which was held on Sunday. In a short address he drew attention to some of the things that have recently taken place in Russia, pointing out how many advantages and torivileges Edglisbmen possessed over the people of Russia, and pressing all present to mike the best possible use of the freedom that they enjoyed. Mr. J. Parkinson, of Salford, was the speaker. He dwelt with ' the drink and gambling evils, urging the meeting to use all possib!e means in its power to bring about a better state of things. Two solos, " Children asleep " and " The promise of life." were very ably rendered by Miss M. Collin. Mr. B. Wadsworth was the accom- panist, and Mr. P. Deady and Mr. T. Taker also took part in the meeting. The usual meetieg of the Wycliffe P.S.A. was held on Sunday last, when Mr. R. Lewis presided and spoke upon "Practical helpfulness." Mr. A. Barbery, of Oldham gave the address and spoke upon the beauties of art and the great wonders of Nature. He urged those present to re id works upon history, which would greatly help to make the home bright and happy. The secretary welcomed one new member (total 529) and ' ' proposed a vote of congratulation to Mr. and Mrs. Yonge upon this, their 29th anniversary at Wycliffe. As their presidcw: they took a great interest in him upon this occasion. This was also his 43rd anniversary as a niinister. Mr. A. Cotton and Mr. J. Owen also took part in the meeting. Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ.

div.head: Stockton Heath New Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Stockton Heath New Wesleyan Church.

The opening services in connection with the new Wesleyan Church at Stockton Heath, were continued on Sunday, when the preacher throughout the day was Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P.. who at the morning and evening services addressed crowded congregations. A musical service was held in the afternoon over which Councillor Brough presided. A number of selections were ably given by an orchestra under the conductorship of the choirmaster (Hr. Penketh), and sacred solos and quartettes were given by Mr. A. Griffiths, Mr. E. Pierce, Miss Griffiths and Miss Woodward. The choir sang the " Hallelujah chorus " " Glory in Excelsis " and " Break forth into joy in a very creditable manner. Tn the evening the orchestra again gave special selec- tions and the choir rendered the anthem " The title." Mr. A. Griffiths was responsible for a well sung tenor solo. The collections for the day were in aid of the building fund and brought the total amount realized by the opening services up to £6O. During the week the moveable screen which will divide the church from the Sunday school has been erected and reflects credit upon the foresight of those who advocated its construction, as on special occasions the ordinary seating accommoda- tion of the church can be doubled.

Mr. BALFOUR gees THE GREAT DECEPTION. to Newcastle next week to address the National Union of Conservative Associations, and an attempt is to be made to drag him over to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S side once and for all. The National Union was Protectionist before Mr' CHAMBERLAIN. As Mr. CHAPLIN points out in a long resolution of which he has given notice, it has been passing resolutions of a Protectionist character since 1887. It grows more careful of its phraseology as it becomes older; but its demandS remain the same. The resolution of Mr. CitArart asks for " a re-adjustment of taxation whieb' without increasing the cost of their food to the poorer classes of this country, will tend to secure fairer treatment of British man' facturers by foreign nations, will prevent the practice of dumping, and largely increase reciprocal and preferential trade between the different parts of the British Empire." This is the CHAMBERLAIN gospel in a revised version. If yoti are to give preference to our Colonies, said lvir• CHAMBERLAIN- at the beginning of his campaign' you must put a tax on food. This policy ha.s net .‘ caught on," and so it has been changed to tenet unexpected circumstances. There can, of course, be no preference without the taxation of food in its most important and substantial items; but Mt' CHAMBERLAIN and his followers do not admit this any longer. Their proposals are founded on an" fenced round by deception. Taught by manY elections that the people will not tolerate the ides of food taxation, they now have the effrontery to pretend that the raising of the price of food is something against which their policy is portion- larly directed. This shifting of the ground this evasion of the points at issue, the one constant feiture of the Chamberlainit agitation. The typical instance is connected Witt old-age pensions. "I would not look at the matter*,
I
I

said the raging and tearing campaigner, "unless i felt able to promise a large scheme for the pro- vision of pensions." But this was three years ago, and much water has passed under the bridges since then. "I do not propose to make the ques- tion of old-age pensions a part of the programme of tariff reform," Mr. CHAMBERLAIN now declares. And so the chameleon policy goes on changing, according to the surroundings of the moment. It is the evident determination of the delegates Who are to assemble at Newcastle to make Mr. BALForrn place his hands within those of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and swear to be his man. There was a time when Mr.o Eterixs abondoned his demand for a tax on corn, and took up with bimetallism as a new plaything. He soon afterwards entered the Cabinet. Being again a free man, he proposes to exercise on the Prime Minister that compulsion Which the Prime Minister once brought to bear on him. At the Albert Hall in June last Mr. BALFOUR said to the delegates of 1,700 Unionist and Con- •servative Associations that our Fiscal system is "no longer adequate or fitted to our needs." He may have meant nothing in particular; but Mr. CHArtati insists on attaching a definite meaning to his words, and, in fact, claims him as a follower Of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. The point is driven home by an independent resolution of which a Mr.TirP ER has given notice. It declares "that there is no vital iflereice between the policy of the Prime Minister and that af Mr. CHAMBERLAIN," and gives its approval to both. Mr. BALFOUR is supposed in some quarters to be an exceedingly sensitive man. If he in any way deserves this reputation, the pro- ceedings of the National Union of Conservative Associations should tuuch him to the quick. He has been pretending to the nation and to his own immediate followers that his views are not those of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. The gentlemen who have prepared resolutions for the National Union tell him frankly that they do not believe him. Under the circvmstanceg, it should he exceedingly diffi- cult to carry on the great deception any longer ; and indeed, for a man of Mr. BALFOUR'S alleged sensitiveness, quite impossible.

man Bolton has been elected to the Mayoralty of Warrington, and we have to congratulate him on his re-accession to that important office. During the past two years the dignity of the Council has fallen to a lower level than ever before, and while the blame for this cannot altogether be laid upon Alderman Bolton yet it has been within his power to have tnaintained a better standard of debate. Only last week, Alderman Tinnion in seconding the vote of thanks to his Worship laughingly twitted him ?nth being the most loquecious Mayor he ever .snew. This was a perfectly true and justifiable Charge. Alderman Bolton's worst fault is that of descending into the arena—we had almost said bear_pit—when the discussion waxes fast and furious. This is just the time when he should refrain from personal argument with his Council lots and endeavour instead to maintain order and some semblance of Parliamentary etiquette in debate. Warrington has not had a more industrious 'Mayor in recent times, but it cannot be said that be has been a pattern Mayor in other respects. There is time and opportunity for Alderman Bolton to improve and we hope he will commence by repressing his desire to have "his say," and instead studiously endeavour to wield the baton of authority with dignity and impartiality.
For the ,third year THE MAYOHALTY. in succession Alder

The splendid success LIBERAL RELAXATIONS. Of last (Thursday) evening's smoking concert and prize distribution at the Liberal Club was evidence of the enthusiasm which is inspiring all ranks of the party in Warrington. Much has been done of late years to encourage the social side of political work and these efforts to bring Liberals more closely into touch with each other have met with due appreciation. The chief object of Thursday's gathering was the distribution of prizes gained in the bowling handicap held during the summer. Mr. A. H. Crosfield whose interest in all healthy recreation is well known, discharged " this duty and took occasion to deliver an interest- _ . . . . _ .

speech, -touching briefly but effectively upon imperial politics. Free Trade, of course, will be the great issue when the battle comes and Mr. Crosfield gave several illustrations of the fallacy of the argument that our trade is dwindling. The most convincing of these to a Lancashire audience affected the staple industry of the county—cotton—which, despite Mr. Chamber- lain's gloomy predictions, is enjoying a period of Welcome prosperity. It is certain that Lancashire Will not depart from the policy which lies at the root of our commercial success, and there is every indication that Warrington will give its verdict for Free Trade, retrenchment and reform.

Alderman Tinnion ALDERMAN TINNION AND has been reading THE " EXAMINER:' "between the lines" of the " Examiner" and drawing conclusions. This is rather a danger- ous procedure, and particularly so when the results are made the subject of a public utterance. The -Alderman, who is, of course, chairman of the Liberal executive, took the opportunity last night of defending that committee in regard to the municipal elections. Thus far, he was quite Within his province, but in alluding to the "Examiner "—if this were necessary—we think he Might have confined himself to what was actually said in our editorial columns. The Alderman's remarks were as follows: "Certainly the Observer and the Guardian 'condemned them and he was not quite sure whether, after all, reading b3tween the lines, they were not condemned by their own Liberal paper the Examiner.'" There is a sort of suggestion here that the "Examiner's" attitude towards the Liberal cause had been of a doubtful character. This we emphatically deny. The " Examiner " has for over thirty years unswerv- ingly and enthusiastically advocated the principles of Liberalism and given the warmest support to the party with which it is allied. So much it may always be relied upon to be and do. But surely such a policy does not preclude the exercise of that inalienable right which, as representing in some Small r deee the free press of this country, we undoubtedly possess of occasionally criticising in all charity the conduct even of our friends. After the election, when the electoral chances of the Liberal nominees could not be prejudiced, we ventured on a little candid, ad we believe whole- some, criticism of Liberal tactics. This is, we think, the time for profitable introspection if the 2auses which contributed to the defeat of the ,Liberal candidates are to be understood and Profited by in a wiser guidance in political matters.
