Chairman : That's to-day; you're in a hurry,aren't you? Applicant: There's no time like the present. chairman: You can have the certificate.

* * * Is there to be work for the workless ? The unem- ployed problem has the sympathy of the Prime Minister. What good is sympathy to a starving man, woman, or child? We must have something practi- cal ; and if he cannot, in his wisdom, suggest the means, it is time that we had some one at the head of the Government who can.

* * * An analysis of the voting strength of parties on the Town Council is, at the present time, interesting. There are 19 Conservatives and 12 Liberals, counting heads politically, while the reu. aiting five are more or less independent. The Non-Traders, of course, draw from all sides, and roughly speaking their voting strength may be stated at 18, or exactly half the Council.

Further disruption! The chief organizer of the Tory Parliament, Captain Lionel Wells, R.N., has resigned. Tariff Reformers have much to be thankful for. We were led to believe that the Conservatives were such a happy family, but first one member and then another leaves to find a new home. No one, but the old folks, will be left soon, It is sad to see such I a breaking up of old friendships. * * Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P.. one of the really grand old men of the House of Commons, concluded his visit to Penketh on Tuesday. During the time he has been in the district, Mr. Cameron has worked hard for a man of eighty. He is essentially a man who delights in living laborious days, and the very warm apprecia- tion everywhere of his eloquent and lofty sermons, addressee and speeches is the best reward he would desire.

_ * * * Our Conservative contemporary naturally extracts much comfort and consolation from the defeat of the three Liberal 'candidates at the Municipal elections. It is quite a mistaken notion, however, to deduce from these results that there is a decline in Liberalism in Warrington. There are much more reliable indications that when imperial issues are in the balance the Liberal poll in Warrington will reach a record figure. The rallying cry has only to be raised and Warriopon will fullow ! * * For a few weeks immediately following the Musical Society's opera performances there has, each season, been an unmistakable slump in local entertainments. Parr Hall ventures, in particular, have suffered to a remarkable extent. On Tuesday and Wednesday evenings this week the combined audiences at Parr Hall for the "Gems " entertainment probably did not exceed 100. Yet the " show " was both clever and refined ; it was well-advertised and the charges were reasonable ; but the public stayed away. * _ *

In the current number of "Dawn," Alderman Bennett has a dignified and appreciative poem on the late Sir Henry Irving which opens with the following verse "Into Thy hands, 0 Lord, Lord into Thy hands," Sooner or later, each of us must fall ; And, now, "the noblest" actor "of them all," Whose fame has spread through all our English lands, No more behind the flaming footlights stands To mimic Death's pale form, so gaunt and tall; No longer comes, however we may call, To take the plaudits which his skill commands. * *

It is estimated that - A hat trimmed between two hundred with tiny ye 110 w million and tlir e e ducklings is the very Ii undred million latest thing. in milli- birds perish each nery. It is to be year to trim the hats seen in the window of the women of the of a shop in the West world.---" The Animals' End of London.— Friend." London Paper. * * * Here and there, in the town, is to be seen some slight evidence of the operations of the Beautiful Warrington Society. With the last few days a number of tubs containing evergreens have been by the agency of Mr. I. T. Williams, placed round the cannons in front of Arpley Station. At present they only serve to make the gloominess of the surroundings more apparent, but in course of time, when they have been reinforced by more greenery, the spot will, we hoPe, appear a veritable oasis in the desert. Mr. Will Crooks, M.P., has been giving his views on the possible solution of the unemployed problem to a London daily. He would make a beginning by the institution of the following schemes : —l, Reclaiming the Wash, with the aid of 2,000 men for ten years ; 2, Protecting the foreshores of the Thames and build- ing sea walls; 3, Making new roads, fit to march troops on, and suitable for motor car traffic. Item number three suggests a certain amount of contempt for the existing roads ! * * "In the developing and perfecting of our Christian character, struggle and conflict are involved. The battle is real, and right on to the end ; and it is this personal combat with evil that develops the muscle and fibre of our spiritual manhood. It is in the storm and stress of life that the value of our character is tested and determined."—These are the words of Sir George Williams, the founder and president of the Y.M.C.A. movement, who died at Torquay on Monday last. Through his instrumentality, the institution rapidly developed, and has now branches in all parts of the world, with a membership of over 700,000. The loss of such a public benefactor is both national and international.

* * * The attacks upon sehooltnasters which have appeared in the "Westminster Gazette" lately, and especially an article by Mr. H. G. Wells, remind a correpmdent that Lamb makes almost exactly the same charges as Mr. Wells does against the schoolmaster: ‘: He is awkward and out of place in the society of his equals. Tie cornea like Clulliver, from among his little people, and he cannot fit the stature of bis understanding to yours. He cannot meet you on the square. He wants a 'point given him like an indifferent whist player. He is so used to teaching that he wants to be teaching you. . . . The jests of a schoolmaster are coarse, or thin. They do not tell out of school. He is under the restraint of a formal or didactive hypocrisy in company, as a clergyman is under a moral one. He can no more let his intellect loose in society than the other can his inclination. He is forlorn among his coevals ; his juniors cannot be his friends." * * ! Mr. S. Gough seems to think he has a special mission to attend Local Government Board inquiries and object to Corporation loans. We never knew his authority for the work before Tuesday, when he explained that be appeared "as a public unpaid servant in the interests of the ratepayers." The loan in question was for the cost of private street making ' and Mr. Gough's persistent questioning was of a some- what aimless charac+er, so much so that he was snubbed by the Inspector. A snub or two has, how- ever, little effect on the pachydermatous bide of Mr. Gough. In his complaint of the quality and want of uniformity of the setts used in paving many streets in the town we sympathise with him, though the matter was not one that concerned the inquiry. Our street- paving is shockingly had, and we venture to extract hope from the Borough Surveyor's statement that in future he hopes to be able to keep to one standard and quality of sett.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Notice. The Warrington "Examiner" is now published on Friday afternoon, price one penny, and is on sale at the various newsagents at about 4 o'clock. Should any difficulty be experienced in getting the paper the proprietors will undertake to deliver a copy at any address in Warrington by 5 o'clock on Friday after noon without extra charge. Address all communica- tions to" Examiner Office," Bewsey-street Warrington PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—AdVt. Coming Events. A public meeting under the auspices of the Stockton Heath Liberal Association will be held in the Hall Cale Assembly Room on Wednesday evening. The speakers will include Dr. Hodgson, Crewe, vice- chairman ,of the Cheshire County Council Education Committee, Mr. A. J. King, prospective Liberal candi- date for the Knutsfcrd , Division, Mr. H. Roberts, and Mr. W. Madden. The ch.ir will be taken at 7.45 by Mr. W. H. Sherburn. The annual sale of work in connection with the Latchford Baptist Church will be held on Thursday next and will be opened by Councillor Brough. The Foreign Missionary Anniversary will be cele- brated at Wycliffe Church on Sunday by the holding of special services. In the evening an address will be delivered by the Rev. W. W. Stephenson, from Gooty, India. On Tuesday evening a public meeting will be held in the Memorial Buildings, when an address will be delivered by 'alr.Stowell Ashwell from Madagascar. Messrs. Crosfield's hand quartette will give selec- tions of music to-night (Saturday) at the popular concert in Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom. The concert programme will also include an exhibition of living pictures. The anniversary services in connection with St. John's Presbyterian Church will be held on Sunday, when the preachers will be the Revs. J. L. Milne in the morning, and J. Glover, of Risley, in the evening. A public meeting in connection With the Free Trade League will be held in the new Independent Methodist Schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Mr. Frank Southern of Manchester will give an address on "Tariff Wars " illustrated by diagrams. The speakers will include Dr. K. E. Markel. Mr. L. Greening will preside. The first subscription concert of the season in con- nection with the Musical Society will be held in the Parr Hall on Wednesday, November 22nd, when Sir Edward Elgar's " King Olaf " preceded by Grieg's " Peer Gynt "suite will be presented. The plan will be opened to subscribers at Messrs. Pearson and Payton's, Ltd., Bridge-street, to-day (Saturday) and to the general public on Wednesday next. The big Liverpool Dio3e,san Tempe-ance B tzaar , will be held in St. George's Halt, Liverwol, on November 21st. 22nd, and 23rd. Amongst the 120 patrons and patronesses are the Earls and Countesses of Crawford, Derby, Latham, and Mum. That e will be fifteen stalls served by upwards of 200 ladies repre- senting Liverpool, Bootle, Southport, Birkdale, Orms- kirk, Widnes, Warrington, St. Helens, Newton-le- Willows, fluyton, Roby, etc. The openers on each day respectively will be the Countess of Darby, Lady Hoyden, and Mrs. W. Gamble, and the chairmen the Earl of Derby, Sir Thomas D. Royden, Bart., and Mr. Alexander Guthrie. There will be numerous concerts, entertainments, elocutionary recitals, kinemato,graph, etc. Arrangements have been made with the principal railway companies having their termini in Liverpool and Birkenhead for reduced fares on showing bazaar tickets.

The Thewlis Charity. The annual distribution of blankets and warm clothing to the poor and deserving people of the borough took place on Saturday at the Charitable Investigation Society's headquarters in Bank-street, under the direction of Mrs. Harrison. Nearly 80 cases were relieved, the amount expended being a little over £l2. The trustees are Mr. E. A. White, Mrs Harrison and the Mayor for the time being. Donation to the Infirmary. Mr. Robert Needham, Bextou Lidge, Knutsford, employer of Joseph Hewitt, stud groom, who was injured by being kicked by a horse at the Walton Show has forwarded a cheque fir £lO 10i., to the secretary of the Warrington Infirmary and an exprersion of his thanks for the excellent manner in which Hewitt was treated in that institution. Hewitt was only discharged last week. " Y " Branch B.W.T.A. The first of a series of members monthly meetings was held in Wycliffe Assembly Hall on Wednesday evening at 7.11 i. Miss Dutton gave a helpful and stimulating address. She encouraged the girls by telling them of her early experiences in Temperance Work showing them that they need not be discour- aged, even by apparant failure, as often unexpectedly good results came from it. The musical pare of the evening was kindly contributed by the Misses Gornall D. Fairclough, A. Beswick, and Hibbert. WASHING AND WRINGING MACHINES try 3. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55 Bridge-street, Warrington.— The Savings Bank. A special meeting of the trustees and managers was held at the Bank, Buttermarket-street, on, Tuesday morning, for the purpose of considering rules for the Special Investment Department which were unani- mously adopted. Mr. William Long presided, and there were also present the Hon. and Rev. C. E. Crass Revs. J. Davies, T. W. Barber, John Yonge and J. F. Matthews, Captain Withiugton, Messrs. J. Geddes, C. White, J. Heplierd, W. Tinsley, W. Richardson, T. B. Carter, J. L. Smith, J. Ifingland, H. Wood, and J. S, Hill. PUBLIC BEIVEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. • Show of Chrysanthemums. On Sunday last Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart.. threw open the grounds at Walton Hall to enable the public to view the excellent show of chi ysanthemmns. On account of the inclement weather, comparatively few availed themselves of the opportunity, but those who braved the elements were amply rewarded by the ex- cellence of the display, the blooms being at present at their best. There was also a creditable show of begonias, geraniums and salvia, which rendered the visit additionally pleasing. The grounds were again thrown open on Thursday, and the privilege will again he extended to the public to-morrow (Sunday) after- noon.

Asx for Cm/TN' GUAM'S HICIAT-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. Young Helpers' League. The members of the Warrington Branch of the 'Voungyelpers' League, On Satprday afternoon, at the invitation of Mrs. J. Rymer Young and Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes held a social gathering at the Old Academy. Mrs. Peter Ilylands, president of the society, oconpied the chair, and delivered a short address, pointing out that whereas other institutions of the same kind mostly required recommendations before chlidren could be admitted, Dr. Bamardo's homes at once took anyone who Was destitute. She j thought the work could not be too highly estimated. (Applause.) Mrs. Itylands kindly offered her grounds !far a sale of work in aid of the homes, which, it is ',hoped will be held next June. Miss Bessie Dutton, moved, and Miss Annie Williams seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to Mrs. Itvlands for her presence and kind offer, arid to Mrs. •Havionr and Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes for a number of musical items which they contributed. Crosfield's Band. A quartette comprising Messrs, G. F. Bedforth (euphonium), F. Bates (second cornet), W. Winstanley (first cornet), N. Whitty (solo horn), and representing this band competed on Saturday last at Failsworth :with 23 other quattettes and carried off the first prize. A remark made by the Judge on his appearance on the !platform is perhaps worth recording. He said "During the playing of these 2-1 there was one band which stood out alone and although I waited for another as good, or better, not one came anywhere near it." It is a romarkable thing that this band should have won no less than three prizes in the space of a fortnight. The other two occasions were the 21st iof October, when at Ti-lam they were nlacel second in I 18 competing hands, and the 28th at Frodsham where they won second place also among 18.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 11, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 11, 1905.
Young.. Free Churchmen's Auxiliary_ Council.

_ _ A well-attended meeting was held in the Bold-street Church Room on Thursday, under the presidency of the Rev. J. S. Hughes, with the object of inaugurating a Warrington Young Free Churchmen's Auxiliary Council. It was unanimously detided to form such society, and the officers elected were Mr. C. E. Parker, president; Mr. S. Ackerly, treasurer ; and Messrs. R, Jones and J. Gray, joint hon. secretaries. A committee of eight was also appointed. The object ,of the Auxiliary is ta educate the young men of the ' town in Free Church history and principles, and with this in view fortnightly meetings have been arranged to be held at the various Free Churches in the town. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good Boors.—Advt. Bird Show at Warrington. .."'"Lovers of birds will this week-end be attracted to the Conservative Club Assembly Room, Sankey-street, where the members of the Warrington Cage Bird Society are holding their annual show. The evert is becoming increasingly popular, particularly amongst local breeders who in the members' section have entered a large number of excellent birds for com- petition. The open classes have attracted the atten- tion of well-known fanciers with the result that some of the finest birds in the country are to be seen. Pigeons are not this year included in thefshow, their place being taken by an exhibition of foreign birds, but in spite of the fact that pigeons have always been very strong, an increase in the total number of exhibits is recorded. Norwich canaries and British birds are again the largest classes in the show. The ' show which opened this (Friday) afternoon will be continued tomorrow. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC takes away that tired feeling.—(Advt.)

_ . Warrington Dramatic Society's Performances. The annual peeformances by the Warrington Dramatic Society will be given in the Parr Hall nest Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, when A. W. Pinero's popular farce Dandy Dick will be produced. In the past the Society has scored some notable successes and havaig a high reputation to maintain the principals have for a long time been closely studying their parts, and two full dress rehearsals before the first public performance will ensure the success of the venture from an artistic point of view. As the performances are in aid of local charities the public should sae that financially the effort will leave nothing to be desired. The cast is a I strong one and will include Miss Kate Brundrett, Miss Margaret Pierpoint, Miss Lucy Wenham, Miss Bessie I Pierpoint, Messrs. S. Wallhead, H. G. Mosley, H. M. Ashton, Geoffrey Dodd, Victor Roberts, R. B. Johnson, and Harold Joseph. Selections of music will be given each evening by Mrs. W. B. Roberts' orchestra. Particulars as to prices, dr.c., will be found in our advertising columns. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK. BRID G E-STRE ET .—Ad v t. Funeral of the late Mr. C. E. Bennett.

The funeral of the late Mr. Charles Edward Bennett whose death occurred last week at the age of 41 years took place on Saturday at St. Thomas' Church. The officiating clergymen were the Revs. H. V. Pigat and H. A. Lester. The chief mourners were Mr. Dunvile Bennett (father), Messrs. William and Randall Bennett (brothers), Mr. H. Betoth, Mr. Benjamin Bennett and Mr. E.Byatt, Macclesfield, (uncles), Messrs. H. Bennett Stockport, W. Bennett, Cnerdly, Baxter Bennett, Ernest Bennett, George Burgess, Ditton, and J. Thompson (cousins), and Messrs. J. Critchley (brother-in-law) A. W. Bennett and E. and T. Critchley • (nephews). In addition there was a large attendance of M 'sonic brethren, deceased hav- ing been for many years a highly esteemed m imber of the Lodge of Lights (148) Amongst those present were Mr. George Wallington and Mr. T. Critchley, Mr. Segar Owen and the office staff of Messrs. William and Segar Owen where Mr. Bennett was employed as an architect, and representatives of the Warrington Builders' Association. Floral tributes ware sent by the following : " Jim and Sissie," William Little and Mrs. Anderson (Earlestown), Mr. Robert Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. IV. Greenhouse, Mr. William Owen, Mr. Segar Owen, office staff of Messrs, William and Seger 0 von, " Herbert and Fannie," Mrs. Preston and family, Mr. and Mrs. E Bradshaw, Mr. and MN. Rogerson, Mr. and Mrs. A. Litton, and " Baxter, Ernest, Tom and Ben." ; H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE Toxic takes away that tired feeling.—(Advt.) Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay. The other evening the Yonne. Ladies' Bible Class in connection with the above Sunday School held an " A.8.C." sale and entertainment, the object being to raise funds to clear off the small balance remaining due on the new organ which was erected in the chapel in the early part of tho year at a cost of £205. The sale and entertainment proved very successful, the sum of £9 2s. 7(1. being realised. As the balance due on the Organ only amounted to £2 6s. 6d., the members cf the class decided that the balance (£6 165. ILd.) should be reserved until such time as the organ was decorated, when the money could be utilized for that purpose. The teachers of the class (Mr. and Mrs. R. C. Tanner) entertained the members to tea, in the schoolroom, on Wednesday evening last. Abaut 55 young ladies sat down to tin, this number • being considerably augmented at the after meeting. Mr. Tanner, on behalf of the class, handed over the pioceeds of the sale', and entertainment to the organ fund treasurer (Mr. F. Atkinson) and the chapel treasurer (lin T. Taylor), both gentlemen suitably res- ponding. A very enjoyable evening was spent. On Thursday evening the Men's Bible Class in con- nection with the Mission, held a charity concert, in aid of Mr. George Hassan (a member of the class, who has been unable to follow his employment for some years, owing to illness). Captain G. R. Crosfield (President of the class) occupied the chair. Mrs. J. Hannan, Miss A. Woodlands, Mr. J. Willett and Mr. J. Humphreys' each efficiently rendered solos, and the Apollo Male Voice Quartette Party gave selections in a pleasing manner. Mr. Handley's Concertina Band was heard to advantage, both items being well received, the audience demanding ; encores. Mr. A. Grounds filled the position of humorist in his well known accomplished style. Mr. F. Atkinson acted as accompanist. As the concert was very well attended (the schoolroom being filled) a substantial sum will have been realised. -During the evening a message was received from Mr. A. 11. Crosfield to the effect that he would be pleased to subscribe to the object of th c ,ncert. KITCHEN RANGES, Fire Gtstes, Tiles So, large stock.—J. S. div.head: -- "THE DANGER OF SECULAR EDUCATION."
div.p: -- "THE DANGER OF SECULAR EDUCATION."

Address by the Bishop of Manchester. Addressing a large gathering in the Co-operative Hall Sankey-street last night (Thursday); the Bishop of Manchester speke at length in defence of tho Education Act. He complained of the desire to exclude religious iastrection from the school curriculum. They were afraid, he said, and he thought ' they had cause to be afraid that the issue of the great educational struggle lay not between denominationalism and undenominationalism but between denomina- tionalism and secularism. Therefore they wel- comed denominational schools of any description, in the hope that it would be long before elementary education was secularized, for they know perfectly well that would mean that a large number of children would never receive any religious instruction at all. (Applause). It was no use saying that they would get it at home because they knew perfectly well that, there were a large number of parents who could not teach them. It was no use saying they could get it in the Sunday schools because those same parents did not care twopence whether the children went to Sunday schools or not. (Applause). They knew that the difficulties wore greatest where the temptations were strongest and temptation was terribly prevalent in the overcrowded homes—homes ruined by drink and immorality, from which the children went into the world without any knowledge of God or of the Lord Jesus Christ. If the elementary schools were made purely secular—what- ever happened the Romanists wonld not give up their schools—the Roman schools would still continue with Roman teachersand many parents who did not like those schools would prefer them to institutions which were purely secullr,and in the end it would become a struggle between the forces of secularism and agnosticism and the forces of Romanisna. (Applause.)—The Bishop was heartily thanked at the dose for his address,

div.head: MAYORALTY.
div.p: THE MAYORALTY.
ALDERMAN BOLTON ELECTED FOR A THIRD YEAR. The Unemployed Act.

Alderman William Bolton is to occupy the Mayoral chair for a third year. The honour was unani- mously conferred upon him at the annual meeting of the Town Council which was held at the Town Hall at noon on Thursday. There was a good attendance, but it was noticed that the Non-Trading Councillors, with one exception (Councillor Chantler), were absent. At the commencement of the meeting the Mayor (Alderman Bolton) presided and there were also present : Aldermen Fairclough (Deputy Mayor), Francomb, Smethurst, Bennett, Tinnion, and Evans, Councillors Craik, Wilkinson, Fulton Smith, Forshaw, Wright, Evans, Ellison, Brough, Wilson, Chantler, Peacook, Burton, Sankey, Maginn and Dr. Joseph, Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (Town Clerk), A, T. Hlla- way (Deputy Town Clerk), John Etirhurst (borough tretsurer), J. G. Gornall (medical officer of health), J. Deas (water engineer), F. G. Ruddock (borough analyst),and G. F. F. White (magistrates' clerk). We are asked to state that Councillors Stott and J Roberts were absent through indisposition.

div.head: ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE ELECTIONS.
The MaYou read the formal return of the recent municipal elections. ELECTION OF MAYOR.
ALDERMAN TINNION AND UNPLEASANTNESS IN THE COUNCIL.

The next business being the election of Mayor, Alder- man Bolton retired from the room. On the motion of Alderman FRANCONII3, seconded by Alderman SxtET- -1 HURST, Alderman Fairclough was elected to the chair. Alderman FRANCoMB then proposed : "That William Rol ton. Esq., be and is hereby re-elected Mayor for the ensuing year, and until the acceptance of office by his successor." die said he was very pleased to have the opportunity of proposing that their preseat A Iyor be asked to accept office again. It was well known to the Council and, he believed, to the town in general taint Alderman Bolton had worked and had done his utmost to give satisfaction in the high position he had occupied. He had had a great deal of work to do, and it was remarkable how he had fulfilled the conditions, and how regularly he had attended almost every committee meeting it was possible to attend. He must have spent a considerable time in doing his duty—in fact he (the speaker) believed Alderman Bolton had put in more attendances than any Mayor had done since the incorporation of the borough. , ; He only hoped the Moyer would have a peaceful year and enjoy good health so that he could once more serve his ! native town withcredit to himself and satisfaction to all ' around. (Applause). Alderman T.r.oums7 seconded and endorsed all that Alderman Francomb had said. He believed that Alder- man Bolton by reason of his post experience land Intimate relations with all the work of the various corn- mittens and the duties that appertained to the Mayoralty was particularly fitted to fulfil the office with entire satis- faction to the Council and to the ratepayers. Probably Alderman Bolton might not have satisfied everyone I during the last two years, but still he (the speaker) 'considered that if they judged Alderman Bolton by comparison he would come out very favourably, because he thought they must form their estimate of his work by the way in which he had carried out the work under very trying and difficult circumstances. He (Alderman ' Tinnion) had had some considerable experience of the various occupants of the chair, but he did not remember one who had had to cope with more difficulties than Alderman Bolton. He considered that under the extra- ordinary circumstances which he had obtained in the !Council Chamber and in the borough, Alderman Bolton , I had discharged his duties in a manner which reflected honour and credit on himself and on the borough. To his mind Alderman Bolton was certainly very satisfactory to a large number of ratepayers— and very important ratepayers. At tlie banquet which he recaotly gave in the Parr Hall there was a re- presentive gathering of which any Mayor of the 3orough might be proud. lie (Alderman Minion) considered the attendance of those gentlemen was a token of their esteem and respect for 'Alderman Bolton. Looking back on the past twelve months marry things had occurred in the Council that all of them would probably regret. He, however, considered that the individual members of the Council were parlays more to blame for the many regrettable incidents than the Mayor. No doubt many of them, and some outside the Council, bad been inclined to judge the Mayor harshly. He was not going to single out individual members but pro- bably as a Council generally they had not given the help and assistance they might have afforded Alderman Balton during those very trying circurnstauces. He would suggest to members of the Council— lard he hoped they would take it in good part—that it would perhaps help to raise the tone of the debates if they would study very carefully the Standing °Mars in or ler that they might know exactly what their own rights and those of the chair ware. Whatever thei r opinions or the opinions of anyone in the Borough had been with reference to the Council or to the Mayor, they could not in any way associate any of those criticisms with the action of the Mayoress. She was a most charming and gracious lady and had done all she could to , help end further the best interests of the town. I Continuing Alderman Tinnion said they all came into the council with some label. They had to do that, he , supposed, to get in. So ne of tnem were lobelled Con- servatives, some Liberals, some Independents, and then they had a sub-division of Independent Liberals, Inde- pendent Labour, Non-Traders, and Independent Non- Traders. That, he took it, was one of those things they I unfortunately had to do when they came before the various constituents, but when they got into the Council he hoped they would all atte:npt in future to drop those labels and to become one whole with the only object of the better goverameat of Warriugton and the conducting of the business in a wav that would re- fleet credit upon themselves, and the Mayor. Ile would appeal to the members generally to drop all those labels and distinctions if they in any way interfered with the proper carrying on of the business of the Council and were at all antagonistic to the best interests of War- rington. Alderman Smarr-Wrier supported the resolu'don which ' Was carried unanimously. Alderman Bolton then entered the Council Chamber and Alderman FAIRcLoUoiI acquainted him with the decision of the Council, expressing the hope that his , third year of office would be pleasanter than the one ' which bad just closed. He thought Alderman Bolton was the right man in the right place, and now that he had beco,re thoroughly accustomed to the work and had the majority of the Council to back him urahe need have: no fear of any unpleasantness like he had last year. ' The MAYOR, having signed the meal declaration,said the Council had his thanks for that renewed exp-ession of confidence in electing him for the third time Mayor of his native town. It was a great honour to hold the position of Chief Magistrate in a town of the import- ance of Warrington, and he appreciated the heavy re- sponsibilities of the office. He had endeavoured to the best of his ability and by the devotion of much time, to discharge his duties to the satisfaction of the Council and of the ratepayers generally. He hoped the business of the Council would be conducted during his next year of office carefully, patiently, and in the best interests of the town. In all probability the action which certain traders commenced against the Muichester Ship Canal Company would be settled during his year of office and he sincerely hoped at the end of that case that all litigation between the Cor- poration and Traders against the Manchester Ship Canal Company would have ceased. (Hear, hoar.) The last transaction in connection with the widening of Bridge-street was nearing completion, aud that improvement he had reason to hope, would before long becompleted. With the heavy rates with which they were now faced they would have to be as economic O. £IS possible, letting all things that could wait, lie over until better days. (Hear, hear). There was every pros- pect of the four large undertakings of the Corporation —Gas, Water, Tramways, Electricity—showing increased profits, and he hoped he was not too sanguine in sug- gesting the possibility of a reduction in the rates at the end of the financial year. In again thanking them for the honour which they had conferred upon him, he wonlal express the hope that the pro- ceedings of the Council would be conducted in a peaceful and friendly manner, and in the interests find for the welfare of the town. (Applause).

div.head: Interesting the School Children.
div.p: Interesting the School Children.

The Beautiful Warringtan movement is making progress. Although some considerable time must elapse before the objects of the promoters are attained a great deal of preliminary work has been done and there is every indication that the townspeople who are interesting themselves in the scheme intend to put forth their best endeavours to make Warrington more attractive. The Society, which was successfully inaugurated in June, is a strong one and has as its president, Colonel Robert Ireland Blackburne, C.B. There are no fewer than thirty vice-presidents, and the Executive Committee consists of the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson (chairman), Alderman Arthur Bennett, Colonel Buckton, the Rey. C. Harvey Cook, Mr. L. Greening, Mr. E. J. Hall, Mr. 0. Lofthouse, Dr. Markel, Mr. F. W. Monks, Mr. J. Moore Murray, Mr. J. Fulton Smith, and Mr. John Upson, with Mr. John Fairhurst as hon. secretary, and Mr. Josiah Longland as bon treasurer. Tha various branches of the Society's undertaking have been delegated to sub-committees. One will pro- niote the laying out of public spaces, planting trees and encouraging the cultivation of gardens, and the pro- vision of wir..dow boxes. Another will aim at the pre- servation of features of interest,the building of artistic houses, Sz., the cleanliness of streets, and the general improvement of the town. A third will address itself to the problem of smoke abatement, while a fourth will seek to work, through the teachers, upon the rising generation in order to discourage deitructiveness and mischief, and to imbue the children with the desire to preserve and maintain all that is beautiful. We are indebted to the Rev Canon Stevenson, who is taking a most active part in the movement, for some interesting particulars of the work accomplished up to date. The membership of the Society now stands at over three hundred, and as it is the intention to make

the organization as representative as possible, anyone who desires to lend assistance is heartily welcomed. The committees which have already commenced opera- tions ere : " The Window Gardening and Tree-planting Committee," "The Streets, Buildings and Vacant Spaces Committee," "The Smoke Abatement Com- mittee," and" The School Committee "and a descrip- tion of the work entrusted to them is given below. WINDOW GARDENING AND TREE PLANTING CONIMITTEE. One of the most important sections of the movement. will take in:hand the encouragement of the provision of trees and plants in the streets, gardens attached to houses, factories_ workshops and institutions

es, 41tutions and also in the waste spaces of the town where possible. The Chairman of the committee is Dr. Markel and efforts will be made to induce the townspeople to cultivate their gardens and introduce window boxes, creepers, and hanging baskets of plants to beautify the streets.

!yr We hear that the employds of one of the large works are displaying a areat interest in the cultiva- tion of plants. Workingmen are being especially encouraged to support the movement, the following circular having been addressed to them : - "The Plants Committee of this society appeals to you to help it in the great work it has in hand, which is to make our town beautiful, so far as that can be done with trees and plants. In place of endless brick and mortar, and patches of barren dirt we want to see 'gardens and windows bright with flowers, walls covered with climb- ing plants and streets planted with trees. The task is huge but full of hope if we help one another. On its part the society will act as go-between to bring those who need advice into touch with those who are able and willing to give it. it will collect from friends of the cause, and distribute to its members, contribu- tions of roots and bulbs, plants, cuttings, and shrubs, many of which would otherwise be wasted. Besides this, it will assist by arranging for the-purchase of things for your garden which it is difficult to buy in small quantities and for want of which gardening in town is often given up as a bad job. The society will thus supply the machinery for mutual help. To encourage healthy competition the committee will hold exhibitions chiefly confined to out-door plants and plants suitable for window decoration. The first of these will be held next spring. Prizes wilt also be given from time to tim 3 for .gardens, window boxes, wall decoration, and for special ingenuity in making cheap devices." There is every reason to believe that this appeal is calling forth a hearty respond. Several offers of tree planting have been received and

div.head: WARRINGTON JUNIOR LIBERAL LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON JUNIOR LIBERAL LEAGUE.
`• The French Revolution and some Effects on English Politics."

The work of the recently-formed Junior Liberal League is naturally, largely of an educational character end the first of a series of lectures was delivered on Monday evening by the Rev. C. Harvey Cook. The meeting was held at the headquarter of the League, Gregory's Cafe, Buttermarket-street, and considering the youth of the Association, was well-attended. The President Mr. Joseph Howes, occupied the chair. Mr. COOK, who spoke under great disadvantage, he suffering from an attack of bronchitis, spoke upon "The French Revolution and sortie of its effects upon English politics." At the, outset he complimented the League on the programme they had prepared. Proceeding with the address he quoted as a motto words , from Gladstone "Be inspired with the belief that life is ' a great, a noble calling, not a mean and grovelling thing to be shuffled through as welcan, but a lofty and exalted destiny." (Applause.) They were making a serious effort to acquaint themselves with historic and contemporary politics. That was well; it was as it should be. Politics were worthy or strenuous struggle. ro use Milton's fine phrase, politicians ought " to scorn delights,and live laborious days." The science of government was yet in its infancy, and we still worked too much by empiricism and rule-of-thumb. Our state was managed and run on the principle of "getting through," not on the sound basic principles of know- ledge. The art of government was yet very rudimentary, and we obtained our State ends not by processes of well-reasoned and scientific inductions, but by experimental and rule-of-thumb deduction. The history of the French revolution, said Mr. Cook, be :an not with Napoleon, but with Louis XIV in 1561. Continuing, Mr. Cook ably sketched the growth of the revolutionary spirit from that period until it reached its height in the reign of Louis XVI. He also graphi- cally described the 'meteoric career of Napoleon I especially denoting attention to his wonderful military ! successes. Leaving the French revolution, the speaker ! went on to refer to its influences on English politics. For 50 years prior to the repeal of the Corn Laws a Tory Parliament held sway. The Liberals were out of power' for a half a century, from 1780 to 1830, all through the fermenting and spasmodic changes of Continental , politics. England w_..s in the hands of one party. The state of English politics during that 50 years of Tory ! Government did not make pleasant reading. Whether i the Whigs would have done much better he did not know. i The nation was discontented, and the people took upon I themselves to manifest their sentiments to the King (George ITT.) in Hyde Park in person. The cry " No King " was raised. The Government brought in a Bill to make it unlawful for meetings to be held in which grievances were to be discussed unless the assembly was called together by public advertisement, attested by the signatures of seven resident householders. Fox impugned that Bill. The people had an inalienable right to gather together to discuss their grievances. Revolutions were not owing to popular meetings, but to the tyranny which was exerted to enslave men. But fear of the people, and not trust in them, I carried the Bill through, though somewhat modified. History repeated itself then as now. One represented ' the situation of the country as replete with the most arduous duties, and almost verging on ruin ; the other as full of opulence and resources. Wilberforce had made his motion for the abolition of slavery. The new Parliament met in 179 e. Burke had published his "Thoughts on a Regicide Peace." The invasion of England by the French was feared, and at the beginning of 1797 gloomy indeed was the national out- look. The national debt was going up by leaps and bounds, but the authorities of tho Bank of England proved to the Ministers of State that funds were plenti- ful, yet other imminent (lingers occasioned a great con- sternation. The soldiers and sailors were in mutiny, because of the smallness and the arrears of their pay, and the great watchwords of the French Republic, " Liberty, equality, fraternity " were being circulated amongst the democracy. The influences ot the French Revolution on English politics were beginning to be felt potently. The Government was alarmed. The sailors would not be content with anything less than the sanction of Parliament and the King's proclamation of their demands. Having quelled this naval mutiny, I

the governing authorities turned attention to the mili- tary, and now for the first time "Tommy Atkins " got his full shilling a day. Ireland and Scotland were in disturbance. Riots took place, and home poli- tics were forgotten in the anxiety of foreign ones ; but in the face of common foes wrongs were forgotten, and all classes joined as one to thwart the invader. But he did not come. Wars and rumours of war kept the European world in a state of agitation. A-aerica and France had quarrelled because America desired peace, and would not support Napoleon. Things moved at a tremendous pace. The English Parliament met on February 2nd,1502,t0 take into consideration the overtures of France for peace. In 1801, by the Act of Union, Ireland and England became one. It was hotly fought on both sides. At home provisions were getting to famine prices. The people were " clemmed." Poli- ticians were advising people who could give help never to give bread or flour, but soup, rice, or potatoes. New bread was forbidden to be sold, none being allowed to be exhibited which had not been baked 21 hours. With the famine of food came a debauch of immorality. The dramatic incident of shoot- ing, by a man in the pit, at, the King in the old Drury-lane Theatre took place on May 15, 1800. Riots were generaland disturbances constantly occurred in London. The prices of corn were being inquired iu- to, and already regulations for diminishing consumption and encouraging importations of corn were in vogue. Politicians seemed then, as largely now, lost in a maze. not capable of reducing politics to a science. Paper had an additional import duty placed upon it, and every source which was calculated to bring the people pros- perity was just the source which the Parliament of the time seemed set on ignoring, and yet he was persuaded that the French Revolution bad this influence upon English politics, namely, that with all our failures wel , had worked our way progressively by means of evolution rather than revolution. (Applause). In a sentence, he Ishonld say that the one great desideratum of the French Revolution on English politics was to make those politics work themselves out on the lines of peaceful but struggling, evolution, as over against ied, raging revolution. For 30 years and upwards the French Revolution had the effect upon the major portion of English politicians of making them more austere and , severe than in the nature of things they were disposed to be. English politici ins of the late 18th and early 19th century looked with a sort of paternal benevolence on the democracy. They thought of it ass sort of pettish- tempered child, to whom it was best to give something ,to keep it quiet. (Laughter). They never studied the rise of democracy seriously, and he questioned very much if it was yet studied seriously by the many. So English politicians muddled through, not understanding %hat was written, that the government of the people ' must be by the people and for the people. (Applause). Democracy itself seldom studied itself seriously, or it would never plead for an English revolution along the lines of the French. English democracy seemed to for- get in the glamour which the French Revolution cast over its mind that it was succeeded by one of the most terrific military tyrannies that ever existed. Napoleon's throne was fixed on bayonets, and any throne thus upbrone must, being contrary to the ethics of progress, gradually dissolve and pass away. There were principles at work in politics if only politicians would take some care to discover them. There were laws at work in politics which politicians seemed never to heed, great moral laws, great moral principles, the grasping of which and the grappling with which alone gave a man title to style himself a politician. To- day we were garnering some of the results of the influences of the French Revolution on English politics. Our people were being franchised. Our law' alined at being the same for rich and poor. Politics cc ere taking the right trend. "We see not yet the full day here, but joyous watch the paling night." (Applause) Man must be free, humanity must rise, the sons of men must come in their glory, privilege and caste must I cease. These were some of the great influences which had floated across the channel to us from that terrific page of French history. France had learned that to , tread the people down was the sumo way to raise a revo- lution. England was solving her problems by the lurid glare of that revolution. not without some hint from the people that they, too, would like the French democracy, rise if their just rights were not conceded. Yet English democracy to-day would not occupy the place it did in the deliberations of our Ministry if across the English Channel a hundred years ago the red war of revolution had nut taken place, and our neighbours had not glowed. Other nations had had their periods of revolution, but none had wrought MOTO mightily upon us, nor was that to be wondered at. Only a strip of sea,twenty miles wide,ran between us and the

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 11, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 11, 1905.

r country that was on fire. The juxtaposition could not help but make us hold our breath and ponder our ways. The condition of the labouring and wage-earning classes a hundred years ago was anything but happy. A hun- dred years ago a miner's representative would never have been allowed in the British House of Commo is. Will Crooks would have the door slammed in his face, and John Burns turned out, bag and baggage. We could not live to ourselves, even politically. Other nations affected us and France's flare up illumined the closed minds of England's aristocratic rulers so drestically that ever since they had been sheken in their fah as to the divine right of one class to be the governing power of another. One hoped that as democracy came to its own, it too, would learn that class govern- ment was nat sound government. The Association he was addressing that evening could teach men that the science of government was not a government for a class, but a government, for all. Democracy I.as far from realizing that fundamental basis of all right government. He did not hail government of democracy any more than he hailed government of aristocracy unless it was a government of the aristocracy of intelleet—the only aristocracy he recognized. Mere democracy or aristocre •:3, were both alike nauseaus to him. They had it in their hands to do something towards helping on " Government by the aris- tocracy of intellect." Whether they drew their politicians from the democracy or from the aristocracy, never let class prejudice narrow their sympathies. Democracy was, when properly understood, the whole of the people, not any more its labouring and wage-earning class than its leisured and intellectual class. He could not close his address with better lines than those of Edward Carpenter : Forth then, ye heroes, patriots, and lovers, Comrades of danger, poverty, and sorrow, Mighty in faith, of freedom your great mother, Giants refreshed in joy's new rising morn. Come and swell the song silent now so long, "England is risen and the day is here." (Applause.) Mr. GRAY proposed a vote of thanks to the Rev. Harvey Cook for his lecture. Politicians ought to remember that power was given them not as a thing in itself, but as a thing for good and wise governrinnt. Mr J. HAWTHORN seconded. Referring to the corn- pstrative smallness of the attendance, said that as an organization they must not in any way be disappointed, as it was from small beginnings that great things arose. (Applause.) Mr. GUEST supported the motion and in addition pro- posed a vote of thanks to the Chairman for his services. He thought much of the misgovernment of England was because those whom we elected to govern us did not represent the feeling of the people owing to the fact the people not having studied questions sufficiently did not know exactly what they were asking for. (Applause.) Mr. FORD seconded, He agreed entirely, he said,with the French revolution, believing that great wrongs required strong weasures to right them. (Hear, hear.) The votes were heartily accorded. In replying Mr. COOK impressed upon his hearers the necessity that they should study good literature. It was .lot the quantity which they read which would be of benefit to them but the material whic'i they read. (Hear, hear). He suggested that the League should include some political study in its programme. The following programme for the next few weeks has been arranged :—November 13th, " Ethical aspects of the fiscal question," by Mr. C. E. Parker; on November 20th, " John Knox," with a reference to Scottish politi- cal history, by the Rev. J. L. Milne ; and on November 27th, " The Relation between Labour and Drink " (a digest of the Leeand Raper lecture delivered by Mr. John Burns, M.P.,) by the Hon. Secretary, Mr. Harold Gray. The Association exists to promote political education among young men, arid all are cordially invited. Further lectures are to be given later.

div.head: BLUE BELL INN.
div.p: THE BLUE BELL INN.

_ Mr. A. Browne applied for leave to make certain alterations to the Blue Bell Inn, Horsemarket-street, by including a small saddler's shop, four feet wide, in the Inn. The shop was originally part of the licensed premises, but some 30 years ago, John Piorpoiat, who kept the inn, arranged with a friend to give him as a personal favour, a portion ofithe premises so that he could sell rope or twine on Market days. His applica- tiou was that the shop should be again included in the bar-parlour of the Inn, of which it originally formed a part. If the application were granted the side door which led into the shop would be blocked up. Mr. H. Roberts : Say that the shop has existed for 50 years. I have known it personally for 17 years. The Chief Constable said he presumed that Mr. Browne was prepared with some evidence to show that the shop was originally within the cartilage of the Inn. If he was not he must object on behalf of the police to the application on the ground that it was contrary to public policy to increase the drinking area in the centre of the town which was admittedly already congested with licenses.

Mr. Brown slid he was unable to produce any evidence. The position of the shop however spoke for itself. The granting of the application would confer a benefit upon farmers who met at the Blue Bell inn to transact businass, the present parlour being too small. The Chief Constable submitted that the owners of the premises, having allowed the present state of things to continue for 50 years, had for all time alienated their right to the shop. The application was refused.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
POKER AS A WEAPON

William Harrison, elassmaker, of 55,Back Lord-street, was charged at St. Helens on Monday with wounding with intent, by means of a poker, John Smart, carte; of ss, Lord-street.—Mr. Etherington (Chief Constable) said that the prosecutor bad some words with his house- keeper on Saturday, and he decided to go to live in Cowley-street. About half-past eight on Sunday night Smart took his box on his shoulder and went .off to Cowley-street. As he was passing Harrison's back yard door Harrison came out and said, " Are you going like that ? " He then pushed the box off Smart's shoulder and struck him two or three times on the head with what he believed to be a poker. Smart said he fell down in the street on the first blow. When he came to himself, and found blood streaming out of his head, he shouted for the police, and Police-constable Jones attended Whim and afterwards took him to Dr. Reid's. where seven stitches were put in the wound in his head He could not explain why Harrison should attack him, but three or four weeks ago he had some wo ds with him. Harrison called him a" Brummagem pig "and said he would for him when it got dark nights. A girl named Ormcly said she saw Harrison strike the blows. Harrison said he was not gnilty, and called his wife,who said that she never saw her husband go out of the house after they went in, about a quarter to seven o'clock. About three weeks before Smart gave her hnsband a black eye,about a woman.—Harrison was Cent for trial at the Assizes.

div.head: FREE TRADE LEAGUE.
div.p: FREE TRADE LEAGUE.
Public Meeting.

The first of a series of public meetings promoted by the Warrington branch of the Free Trade League was held in St. Sarnabas Schools Rostock street, on Thurs- day evening of last week. There was a fair attendance, Mr. S. Rigby Armitage presiding. The principal speaker was Mr. J. R. Cambell, of Manchester, and there were also present on the platform. Councillor Evaus,Mr. F. R. Roberts,Mr. A. Rathboue and J. Elwell. The Chairman emphasised the importance of holding meetings in support of Free Trade as the protectionists' had been very active in presenting their side of the question. He called attention to the conditions in pro- tectionist countries, as showing the advantages which we enjoyed under Free Trade, and pointed out that in Germany, for instance, the price of meat and commo- dities had risen over CO per cen.t. and that specially hit the working man. In an able address Mr. T. R. CAMBKLL said that even if we gauged the country's prosperity like M r.Chamber- lain, according to the amount of exports, the Protec- tionists' contention that our prosperity was declining was disproved. No country in the world could show any such extent of over-sea trade as we could. One of the greatest arguments for Free Trade was that, first of all, it was for the benefit of labour and afterwards to the benefit of capital while the Protectionist argument they maintained, was first for the benefit of capital and then down to the benefit ,1 of labour, if it was able to get any. Free Trade meant I cheap food and therefore an increased purchasing poA Jr and enabled raw material or anything that was necessary I for our industry to come into the country free and I unfettered. Councillor JAMES EVANS delivered a short address emphasising the advantages men had accrued to the working-classes since the adoption of Free Trade,

Mr. J. Etwer.a moved a vote of thanks to Mr Cambell and said Protection would press most heavily on those least able to bear the burden. Mr. F. R. ItonsaTs seconded. Mr. Chamberlain, he said, was trying to advise them to accept duties on necessaries in lieu, of duties on luxuries. The effect would be that whereas under the present system they were contributing to the revenue of the country, which it was absolutely necessary they should do, Tinder Pro- tection they would simply he putting their money into the pockets of the merchants and dealers and would have to find the national revenue from some other source. He believed that Warrington would prove to be a thorough Free Trade town.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: PAVING OF STREETS.
div.p: THE PAVING OF STREETS.
Application for a Further Loan.
MR. GOUGH IN OPPOSITION.

Colonel A. S. Smith, R.E., held an inquiry on behalf of the Local Government Board at the Warrington Town Hall on Tuesday into the application of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £9,406 to defray the cost of making up certain pri‘ate streets under the Private Street Works Act, 1892. Amongst those present were :—Alderman Smethurst, CouncillJr Skelland, Mr. S. Gough, the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. A. T. Hallaway), the Borough Treasurer (Mr. J. Fairhurst), and the Borough Surveyor (Mr. T. Longdin). The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK made the application on behalf of the Corporation, pointing out that they desired the Local Government Board to allow eight years for repayment of the loan. Originally they asked for seven years but for certain financial ressons,which the borough Treasurer would explain, they desired an extension. The Bonet:nu TREASURER said that by a resolution of the Council the owners of the property where streets were made had seven years granted for the repayment of the street-making account. It took probably a good partof twelve months to prepare the streets. Then, the streets were made before the apportionment of the cost was arrived at, and it therefore meant that eight years elapsed before the Corporation received the last instalments. If the Board would grant an extra sear he thought it would meet all the requirements. The difficulty was that the Corporation had to spend the money before the apportionments were made Mr. GOUGH: May I ask one or two questions? The INSPECTOR: We will go through the whole matter first. .
Mr. Gouu ft : Is it not necessity ths.t we should put a few questions to the Borough Treasurer on his evidence ? The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK : This is not a Court of Law. . .

Mr. GOUGH : Evidence has been given for the pur- pose of obtaiping the loan I vvoald like to ask the Bolough Treasurer what the total indebtedness of the Borough is at the present time. The BOROUGH TREASURER : The total indebtedness of the Borough on October 31st was £1,171,235, less £8,333 which we have in the sinking fund. Mr. GOUGH : Would it not make a difference if the Corporation did not buy the setts. There would be no need to ask for the want year would there ?

The BOROUGH TREASURER : I cannot see that that has any bearing on the question as to length of time. Whoever bought the setts, it would make no difference. The work will certainly take a good share of twelve months to execute, and as the Council have thought fit to give seven years for repayment, it would still take eight years to obtain the whole of the money, whoever bought the setts. Mr. Goucit : You say it will cover eight years, but you won't have to borrow any money till the work is completed, will you ? The BOROUGH TREASURER : We don't find contrac- tors working twelve months without pay. The ordinary arrangement is that they shall be paid monthly. The measurement of the work is taken and they are paid by instalments. t4Mr. GOUGH : Does not the purchasing of setts inter- fere with the loan in a great measure ? The INSPECTOR : I don't think that is very material now. In reply to the Inspector the BOROUGH TREASURER said the outstanding debt included t;2,6i,539 under the Public Health Act. The Boßocoß SERvEYoR said the Paving and Sewer- age Committee passed resolutions theta certain number of passages and streets should be paved on the ground of sanitary conditions and also for the benefit of tbe , owners and tenants of the property. Ten streets and 'GS passages were included in the present loan. Wita one or two exceptions the streets and passages, were similarly paved. There was a standing resolution of the Council that all new streets should have a concrete bed rout inches thick and be pitted with setts either of granite or freestone. The Corporation had in times past experienced great difficulty in obtaining setts owing to the rush of tramway construction throughout the country and they were ;obliged to use sandstone setts as the price of the granite setts had risen from 225. to 40s. Now, however, the price had gone down and all the streets and passages were to be paved with the Winstone or granite setts. The cost was no more than that of the ordinary sandstone sett but the durability was three times as great. Property owners, he considered, were getting the streets paved and sewered at a very reasonable price. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK said six objections to the work had been received and copies were being sent to the Local Government Board. The Corporation were at present engaged in negotiations with the objectors and they had every confidence that in a few weeks the cases would no settled without having recourse to the ma gistrates. Mr. GOUGH :_Yon have not always settled the cases

The TOWN CLERK : We are not infallible. Mr. GOUGH : Complaints have been made for yerrs past that the work is not carried out according specifications. That is one of the objections we are going to raise. The IvsrecTon : That is another matter. We are now dealing with the ouestions as to whether the particular objections are ~zely to be settled or not. I am not going into any back history. Mr. GOUGII : How many of these streets have been paved already ? The BOROUGH SURcEVOR said that none of the streets or passages included in the application had been paved. Mr. Gonott : Have you got any idea as to how many setts will be required for the carrying out of the whole of the work ? .
The Boßouoil SURVEYOR : Somewhere abont 3,000 tons. _
Mr. Got Gil : Will you supervise this work ? The Bortouoit SURVF,YOR :I have a special man appointed to look after that for me—a private street works foreman.

Mr. Goti : Have you any recollection of Coun- cillor Lord asking this question of the Chairman of the Paving and Sewerage Committee— The Deputy TowN CLERK : We are not going into ancient history. The INsPEcTort : No, I don't wish to go into past history. I inquired whether there is any objection to these streets being made. Are there any private owners present? Mr. Gouct-r : Yes : Tam onn.

The iI3N-V-s- CLERK : You are not concerned with these streetsand passages. Mr. Clot:un : The loan is being borrowed on the rates of the town and as a ratepayer I have a perfect right to object. The 'INSPECTOR. .Quite so, but you are not a private owner in any of these streets ?

div.p: A FREE SAMPLE OF
[BY MR. H. WHITIIAII].

A little over twelve months ago -Mr. T. Lawson started a; movement that is haying some very monientous results. Taking his word for the very truth, we find that for several years he had been gradually working out and perfecting a scheme w i hereby he would find himself n a position to throw a bomb of such magnitude as would cause the tt'iole of the American financial world to tremble down to its very foundations. Incidentally, in the forewords of his attack on the Standard Oil Company, he referred to the methods of work of the various Insurance Com- panies. For the few words he uttered in this direc- tion a considerable amount of press matter was hurled at him. Briefly, I may say the charge against him was that of unsettling the minds of a very large port tion of the saying and thoughtful community, and that the work he was doing was criminal. A calm and, in a sense, indifferent answer to this charge wm s that the Press cared little for the people's welfare if it could only increase the bu"-: of its advertising columns, and that he, Mr. Lawson, was content to wait and let that side of his charge take care of Itself, he in the meantime pledging himself to make Mr."Oilfeller" disgorge the whole of his .c.',100,000,000.110w accurately he had sized up the position has been seen during the past few weeks in the revelations made touching at least two of the world's great money making schemes. I refer to the Patent Med:cine fake, and the great Life Insurance swindling companies, to the latter of which ' we may profitably give a little attention. If thereeis one institution with which the ordinary common people come into contact with, which should be held sacred more than any other from the thieving swindling fingers of the get-rich-quick class it is that of the Life Laurance business. It is by means of the small savings of the wage eat-nine', petty shop keepers and small tradesmen generally Sat a way is opened whereby provision can be made for the proverbial rainy day that does certainly come to most, or all families sooner or later. I have not tried to find out how far the Life Insurance Companies of America are ' doing business in England but that they are doing some I know to be so, and therefore I would say that there is no need for uudue anxiet,r, the companies will I not fail to meet their obligations. In Germany steps have been taken already to put the Branch establish- ments through a thorough overhauling. The great trouble in the States is the National Government can do nothing in the matter. Each in,dividual State must take Independent steps, both in State Parliament and State Court. Already some of the State Governors have commenced proceedings, and Mr. Lawson has arranged for mass meetings and Inpe,s to have aII number of State Governors as speakers. It may be asked just here, what is the matter, and l what is wrong ? The aniwer is a very long story,and Iday by day it is being gi zen in the law courts of New York. It seems 0 be aa accepted fact that in all these Insurance Societies there is a criminal wasteful- ness always going on. Palatial building are erected, and are furnished in wasteful fashion. Sky-scrapers in which the chief tenant is the owner. Rooms with- out end having no tenants at all. Banquets of the most costly description at which Presidents and officials with their friends feast all at the policy holders expenss.Palace cars to r'de about the country in, and yachts to skim the ocean wave. The under- l‘ying feature is that the policy holder joins a 'mutual "and he finds the profits going into the pockets of officials. Instead of the policy holders premiums being fixed at reasonable rates and to meet the various special feature of different societies, they are fixed to meet the liabilities caused by premeditated scoundrelism, not the least of which is nepotism of which the two following are examples:—

The chief reason for this state of affairs is found in the enormous increase in the cost of imported articles, and the fact that the small tariff formerly levied went to the Treasury of the Islands and conse- quently the people received the benefits, while now tariff receipts go to the national treasury at Washing- ton. A printing outfit which was bought in the United States under the old system and delivered in Honolulu for sixty-five dollars, to-day would " cost one hundred and five dollars. A sewing-machine now , costs more than one-third more than the same machine ! cost before the Stars and Stripes floated over the island. While all nations were on equal footing, the , over-rich American trusts and monopolies sold their goods in Honolulu as they do in England and other . foreign lands to-day, at a fair profit, but at a far less . price than they impose upon the Americans, because the latter are helpless, owing to the tariff wall, So in Hawaii, as soon as the islanders became the • victims of the American tariff system that exists for the enrichment of the few at the expense of the . many, they had to pay the exorbitrit prices rendered possible only because of the power of corrupt wealth wielded by privileged interests for the continued oppression of the masses. These facts remind us of the recent panic in the ranks of the tariff-fed trusts and monopolies, when some time ag ) the Government merels mentioned its determination to buy such things as might be required for the building of the Panama canal in the cheapest markets. This simple declara- tion created consternation in the camp of the protected trusts and other privileged interests that are fighting for the lion's share of the hard-earned money of Cu) ' American workers. The trusts fear discussion. One j fact brought out by this contro—ersy is sufficient to : explain why the multi-millionaire trust magnates are so fearful of free discussion of the tariff question. The G wernment will have to buy large quanti- ties of Itoel in order to prosecute its I work in the canal. The steel rails can be Ipurchased at twenty dollars per ton. These rails are ! made by the American Steel Trust and are sold at a ; profit in London of twenty dollars, but if the Govern- meat buys the rails of the American Trust in America it will have to piy the same shameful extortion that lis exacted by this robber combini tion from every j American user of steel rails—narnely,from twenty-eight ! to thirty dollars per ton, or from eight to thirteen dollars more than the same rails will cost in London, made by the same Company. This is a fair sample of 1 how protestion works and enables a few men to amass I untold millions at the expense of the American peop'e millions which enable them to control all the political machines select and appoint pretty well all State and Government officials, and to a large extent govern the nation. Well might Mr. Havemyer, the sugar king, say the tariff was the mother of the trusts. I may' state that just now there are a goodly number of State and Federal legislators serving tale in prison for all this corruption. When the inquiry now going on in New York is concluded it is just possible a few more may find their way there. Tnese men are above the law, aid own- ing pretty well the whole of the Press they are masters of the situation. But this sort of business is coming to an end, and the people are wakening up. From the Atlantic to the Pacific, the yellow journals which are the only ones to speak out, are enlightening the people. Some few ministers are speaking out, but as a rule the. churches also are held in bond. The following explains and will account for the corruption that enables men to endow universities and build libraries, " In the years 1903-01 the Midual set aside 200,000d015. in four regular payments of 25,000d015. each year for the use of the " confi- dential fund," which was used for the purpose of influencing legislation and for campaign purposes Out of this fund payments to the National Republican campaign were made. Vice-president Gillette testified that the Mutual Life Insurance Company contributed 40,000d010. to the Republic-an National Committee campaign fund in the last election in 1904. The Mutual contributed 90,0001015. to the Republican compaigns of 1904 and 1900 and 1896 This much the officials admitted. How much more may have been contributed can only be guessed. As in the New York Life, none of these expenditures were booked, and nowhere is tliere to be found a line or curve to tell of the use of a d dliii, of the 200,000d015. turned over to E. L. . Short, ostensibly for disbursements." J. H. WHITFIAM. San. Francisco, October 13th, 1905.

DEAR CHILDREN,

Now that Christmas is approaching I am making arrangements for a grand Christmas series of competitions which I shall announce in a week or two. In the meantime I want you to give me any suggestions, and to the sender of the best idea I will give a large box of Fry's chocolates. So write to me as soon as possible and tell me what you think would be the most suitable idea for a Christmas prize.

I will also give a special prize to the boy and girl who sends me the best essay on the place they live in and what they think of it; so this is a chance for all, and I hope you will all try for the prize.

I have sent a box of chocolates this week to Gladys M. Xendall, as she sent in the first correct solutions to puzzles. Many of you were right, so you must not give up, but try each week, and no doubt in time you will be the lucky winner. I will give a prize to the sender of the first correct solutions to puzzles given below. With all good wishes, from UNCLE NED.

, Dear Uncle Ned,—l am eager to know the answers to last week's puzzles, as I could not find one of the trees, but I could solve the rest. I think I have the correct answers this week, and I hope to be the lucky one. I am glad to see you are • sending puzzles every week, as I look forward to them, and it is a nice amusement for the winter months, when it is too dark and cold to go out in the even- ing to play.—l remain, your loving niece V.P.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing you my second letter hoping you are quite well as I am. I see the number of members have amounted to 356, which pleased me very much, and I hope there whl be a lot more. I have been trying every week to solve the puzzles, but I don't seem to succeed, I have been trying to guess this week's' but I can't guess _them all. Perhaps I shall be successful some week, so I must not give it up. Dear Uncle Ned, I do think it is a lot of people's birth- days this month. 'OAD AND THE FIREWORKS. (Continued.)

As soon as he was gone, one of the fireworks began to talk. "How tiresome toads are," it said. "I'm glad I'm not one. I'd much rather be a pin-wheel. For, though pin-wheels don't live so long, they end their lives in a blaze of glory. And what pleasure they give to those who are watching them, in their last bright moments. Just fancy: I'm lighted, and away I go in a shower of sparks, round and round and round, faster and faster and faster, the children shouting with delight. Then, whizz! in a flash I turn the other way, and round and round and round I go, faster and faster, and faster—" "Pshaw!" rudely interrupted one cf the .ther fireworks. "Pin-wheels don't amount to much. They can be seen only by the few people who are near them, and they have to be fastened to a fence or a tree to be seen at all. Now I am a sky-rocket. I leave the earth- behind me when I am set free, and away I soar like a bird, up, up, up, among the stars. And there I burst into stars, myself,—stars of all the oolours of the rainbow, and so beautiful that the real sky-stars turn pale. And hundreds and thousands of people see me. Yes, hundreds and thousands."
The pin-wheel made no reply. "Yes, hundreds and thousands," repeated the sky-rocket. But all the other fireworks remained silent.

div.head: toad hopped up the porch steps again. _ _ _ _ _ _
div.p: The toad hopped up the porch steps again. _ _ _ _ _ _

. - "And what then?" he asked. "Oh 1 you're back, are you?" said the sky- rocket. "Yes, I'm back," said the toad. "I didn't go far. Not so far but that I've heard all that you and the pin-wheel have been saying. You look down on the pin-wheel because you are going to soar like a bird, do you? And your stars are sure to make the real sky-stars turn pale, are they? And hundreds, yes, thousands of people will see and admire you, will they? Arid what then?"

"Well, what then," asked the sky-rocket. "Why, then, what is left of you will come down to earth again, and it will be nothing but a small piece of wood. And all that will be left of the pin-wheel will be a small piece of wood also. So you see, though you begin in a much grander manner, both end in the very same way." "Good-night," snapped the sky-rocket. " What ?" asked the toad.
" Good-night ! " - "Oh I good-night," said the toad; and down the steps he hopped again, and away to his home near the well.
But he had spoken the truth; for on the next night at that same hour, there was nothing left of either the pin-wheel or the sky-rocket but a small piece of wood. •

div.head: SOMEBODY.
div.p: SOMEBODY.

"Somebody," was a little girl Who had a curious way Of ordering all her friends about, Ten—twenty times a day. "Oh, Mary," she would say, "come here, And brush my hair for me!" And "Jennie, please hang up my dress— See, here's the wardrobe key!" And, "Oh, I've left my fan downstairs; Jo, fetch it,—that's a duck!" And, "Where's my glove? Do find it, dear. Oh, mercy I—just my luck!" Or, "Horrors! There's no water here. Oh, won't you fetch some, Kate?" Or, "Here's a pin; just catch my dress. Please hurry, I am late!" Or, "Lend me, quick, a pen, a stamp; I've got this note to write!" Or, "Whisk my dress off, will you, Bet? This shoulder's almost white." "Come here! go there! do this, or that!" To every one she'd say; And yet she was a charming girl But for this curious way!
