div.head: POPULAR PENNY CONCERTS.
div.p: POPULAR PENNY CONCERTS.
Mr. R. Cameron, M.P. and Wholesome
Recreation.

IThe third of the series of popular penny concerts which was held in Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom on Saturday evening was largely attended and proved a complete success. An exceptionally interesting pro- gramme was submitted ana was highly appreciated. i Songs were creditably rendered by Miss L. Dunn, Miss L. Snelling, and Mr. A. Corrin, while humorous trios by !Messrs. H. Clare, E. Taylor, and J. C. Taylor proved ! very popular. Mrs. H. Haviour pleased the I audience with well-executed violin solos. Mr. Alf. ' Grounds created great merriment with several humorous sketches which were given in his best style. The concert was presided over by Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., who said the popular concert movement was a good one as it provided a counter-attraction to the public-house and the streets. He hoped those who found public-houses a temptation and wandered about the streets would be induced to visit the concerts as he I was sure it would be of great advantage to them. i (Applause). During an interval a short address was delivered by Mr. ROBERT CAMERON, M.P. He said he was glad to see such a large gathering on a Saturday night. He met a great many working men on the Sundays—generally in the afternoon—and he had seen meetings at Liver- pool, Sheffield and, he believed Manchester, of a ; thousand men. He found that workingmen would I come in when the services were less formal and I perhaps more interesting, because they were not the usual chapel round of things. lie did not know why workingmen should not enjoy Chapel as I well as he did, If he beard a true sermon or a true prayer he felt he had been brought in contact wllit ; the highest things man could touch. Saturday night concerts had another advantage in that they showed that people could enjoy themselves without any coarse- ness or low company and, should he add, without ; getting drunk. They could be clear headed, bear some- thing that was really refining as well as amusing, and I feel all the time that they were the better for it and ; would not go home to have a headache in the I morning or, a quarrel before they went to sleep. He was exceedingly anxious that the people of this country and especially the working people—should take advantage of the schooling they had and not immediately they left school close , their books and studies and give themselves up to what he thought was far too common—the ordinary pursuits 'of the mass of workingmen in our time. He believed in physical exercises because we could not have a really , healthy mind unless the body was healthy. Football, ; so far as it developed the muscle, the eye, the elasticity of the body, sharpness and energy was good. Every I boy should play it but eveiy, man when he was approaching thirty should let it alone and do some- thing else. If by the time he was thirty the only excite- ment he had developed was the excitement of football or gambling, he would find he had missad the chief end of being placed in robust health, unless he had risen out of physical excitement to ' mental and moral excitement. When they were past the state of physical excitement,said Mr. Cameron, they should go in for books. Ile could play football as well as anyone present at one time, but after he was twenty years of age he turned his attention to reading and discussing, and purchased every book he could save money enough to buy. He might say that books con- verted him. Thomas Carlyle was his intellectual and I spiritual monitor in the truest and highest sense of the I word. He found higher excitement in those pursuits ; than he had ever found in physical sports. Reading I brought one's hightest nature into play. kle also I enjoyed science when he was young end he I was thankful for it. One might know the history of the world beneath his feet. Age after age was revealed and life after life came up before one, and as one gazed upon these mysteries one realized what changes had come about. Vie had enlarged our idea of the creation of the world within the last thirty years. Why should men and women who had brains to understand what had been revealed pass through life as if they were Hottentots or Blackamoors who had never had education. Mr. Cameron also spoke of the value of art and music and also urged his hearers to try and learn what the poets had to teach them. The poets were the prophets of to-day—the deepest thinkers, the most beautiful of expression, the most refined in thinking, sometimes the wisest and deepest who had solved our highest problems for us. Mr. Cameron concluded his advice to his hearers by saying that without religion they would sink gradually as they got older and they would harden and darken. If they got religion and the steps he had mentioned that led up ; to it,they might rise to be thelideal men and women that God meant they should be when he created them.

div.head: WORKS OF CHARLES LAMB.
div.p: THE WORKS OF CHARLES LAMB.
University Extension Lecture.

IContinuing his course of University Extension lectures 1 on " A trio of English Essayists" the Rev. IV. Lawrence 'Schroeder, M,A.' on Friday evening dealt with the works of Charles Lamb. He pointed out that Lamb's best work was done in periodicals. The miscellaneous magazine in his day was beginning to take the ear of the public, its varied note and skilful inter-reading of , many utterances proving attractive for minds of divers orders. One might say that Lamb's claim to immortality rested on the work done for the transient magazine. It was curious to note that Lamb's work was not very popular with the general reading public, lie was greatly appreciated by the authors of his day but he only slowly came into vogue with the ordinary reader. Dealing with "The Essays of Ella" the lecturer pointed out that the name Elia was taken from an old Italian clerk at the South Sea House. After all, we might talk a great deal about Lamb's life and feel that he was an admirabi• 1 man in many ways, hut the best introduction to Lamb was the essays. They put us in closer relation with the man than any mere biography could effect. They were frank expressions of likes and dislikes, sympathies and antipathies ; yet through them all we discerned a reverent reservation of certain kinds of intimate ! thought. He never fooled about religion. His essays exhibited powers worthily directed to the deepening of human sympathies, but there was no attempt' to be I highly moral or didactic. Lamb made his appeal to 1 our hearts in a tender graceful way, hiding deep I thoughts and sincere emotions in the.pathos that bordered on tears and smiles. There was no parade of learning for the sake of learning and there was none of the lofty superiority orhigh stiltedness of De Quincey,but there was a beautiful sincerity of mind and soul which allowed the reader to enter straight away, without mis- giving, into strong affectional relations with the author. ‘Vithout sentimental gush, Lamb made us feel that he genuinely liked his readers. The man was really sin- cere. We drew near to him, and the more we read the more we liked him. At the end if we were something of his (the lecturer's) temperament we felt that despite all Lamb's faults and the awkward fact that he sometimes did disreputable things, we just .wanted to put our arms round his neck and give him a good hug. One was struck by Lamb's mastely of detail. 1 The things of common life were not despised, but were glorified JD cheerful phrase. His detail was not a hap- hazard jumbling of oddities, but the result of a true, literary constructive power. The apparent artless- ness of his work was a tribute to his skil

The Liberal party—or probably to be more he makes such statements.—Yours faithfully, ; correct the Executive Committee of the Liberal party, F. MERLIN, that body of men who were so wicked in the eyes of (Electoral Superintendent 1.0.G.T.) some people and who did all kinds of things that were Firth Place, Warrington. I absolutely wrong and seldom did anything that was right—(laughter) —had been charged recently witb attempting to run candidates for the Town Council with the object of testing their machinery to see if it was in order for the general election. He gave AN EMPHATIC DENIAL to that statement. (Hear, hear.) As a matter of fact, those whom he might call the expert advisers on electioneering matters, said it was undesirable so far as they could, to do anything that would take away the attention of the voters from. the momentous issues that would be placed before the constituency when the general election was at hand. What had they done that was such a crime in the eyes of some people? The Execu- tive Committee met—he supposed they had a right to meet and discuss their business, and decide what they would do—and they had this matter amongst others under consideration. After discussion they decided that they might simply say to the Wards that in the opinion of the Executive Committee it was desirable, 'providing the Ward Committees thought fit, to contest the whole of the various seats for the Town Council at the November election, but it was in no way an attempt to force any particular kind of policy, either aggressive or otherwise, upon the Ward Committees. What did they do ? Surely they had a right to contest Bewsey Ward where they had a Liberal representative. Surely they had a right to defend their ward. But what happened in Town Hall Ward ? The gentleman who twelve months ago was elected to represent that ward was not quite sure in his politics. At any rate other people were not quite sure of them, because he was opposed by the Conserva- tive party. Therefore he took it the Conservative party at any rate did not know that Me. Benson was a thoiough-going Conservative. Well, the Liberals put up a candidate against him. In Howley Ward they had a Liberal who was a Non-Trades but none the less a Liberal as the representative. He declined re-election and they nominated another Liberal in his place. What had they done as a Liberal Executive that should bring down all the wrath of those indignant gentlemen, of the Conservative Press—he was going to say of the whole of the Press in Warrington? Certainly the" Observer" and the" Guardian "condemned them and he was not quite sure whether after all,reading between the I ines,they were not condemned by their own Liberal paper the " Examiner." He did not think the Executive had
DC*TE ANYTHING_ VERY WRONG.

Candidates must go into the Council Chamber with some label, and he had yet to learn and know that the label of Liberalism was a label that any man need be ashamed of. He, for one, was not ashamed of it. He contended that the Council and the Councils that had preceded it had been composed on the Liberal side of men who had done a great deal for the betterment of Warrington, and as a matter of fact on the various committees they were the men who did the most intelligent work. At any rate they did the work in the most intelligent way and they were above Sue- picion, and he thought no one need attempt to throw a stone at the Liberal party because they sought to put members in the Council because they were Liberals. He had always contended that, provided the two men were equal, if a man was a Liberal and a Pro- gressive he was better than a man who was a Conserva- tive and of reactionary tendency for town's affairs. Sometime ago the same parties who found fault to-day with the action of the Liberal Executive found fault with them because they did not do what they had done to-day. They found fault with them because they were parties, so their critics said,to a compromise. Personally he was NO PARTY TO THAT COMPROMISE, and never had been. He never sympathised with it,and never took any part in it at all. But where was the logic of those gentlemen ? They made a great noise because some years ago, they did not contest the ward as a Liberal Executive or as Liberal ward committees, and now they did contest them those gentlemen found fault with them and said they had done wrong. It seemed almost impossible to please these gentlemen, but he for one was not ashamed of the candidates they put forward. He thought they would bear comparision very favourably with the candidates who were elected. (freer, hear.) Therefore he was not there to apologise for any action they had taken but to defend the action of the Liberal Ward Committees and the Executive. He only regretted that their action was not more successful. They must not let the Tory party or any other party in Warrington think the efforts that were made an November Ist were I the efforts that would be made when they had a general election. (Applause.) It was a different class of voters to which they had to appeal at the general election and it would have been ridiculous for them to attempt, sup- posing it had been true, to run their machinery to see how it would act when at the general election it was intended for a different kind of work and an altogether different kind of election. Alluding to the concert, Alderman Tinnion said it was desirable for the interests of the social side of Liberalism to have a room better adapted to concerts and other entertainments. (Hear, hear.) They as a club were very much indebted to Mr. Crosfield for his generosity and for the very lively interest in everything that was for the good of the Liberal party and particularly of that club. When he said the Liberal party, he meant for what was best in the interests of the whole of Warrington generally, for he contended that Liberal and Progressive measures would do the most good ultimately to the greatest number. (Applause). Mr. J. E. Wattront seconded and said Mr. Crosfiel's generosity seemed to be unbounded. Prizes were given year after year to encourage bowling amongst the mem- bers, but above all they desired to thank Mr. Crosfield for his presence that night which they especially esteemed. He (the speaker) did not know any man in his time or at any rate since the loss of their old and revered friend Mr. McMinnies who had so completely won his way to the hearts of the townspeople as Mr. Crosneld. (Applause.) When the great battle came they hoped he would he returned triumphantly at the head of the poll. (Loud applause.) Mr. Warren pro- ceeded to refer to the merits of bowls as a recreation and paid is compliment to the manager for the care he had taken of the green. The vote was accorded with great enthusiasm. MR. CROSFIELD AND IMPERIAL POLITICS. Mr. CROSPIELD in reply said he did not know why a vote of thanks should be proposed to him for that evening's proceedings because all he had done was to sit there and enjoy the delightful music they had had. The last time they had a concert in that room he said they had fairly beaten the record. But beautiful as were the decorations on that occasion and excellent as was the music, they bad a still more beautiful room and a more perfect concert that night. (Applause). It was a very happy thing that from time to time they could meet together not alone to talk politics, as they had to do on so many occasions, but to combine music with their Political education, just as the ancient Greeks used to make music and gymnastics the basis of their education. After all they at that club were following upon the lines of the Greeks in another particular. because if they did not call bowls altogether a gymnastic sort of exercise, it was a very healthy farm of outdoor sport and he sincerely associated himself with what had fallen from the Chairman when he said that bowls was the most accessible game for all of them Vlt was the first gime he (Mr. Crosfield) ever played in I his life, and his father was very keen on it. He (the speaker) had played lots of other games since, but he hoped to be associated with bowls as long as he lived. (Hear, hesr.) When a man got smitten with golf it was a bad case. (Laughter.) He had to go through the whooping cough, the measles and the scarlatina— (laughter) —and be lay awake at night thinking of the "puts "he had missed, (Laughter.) If it were not that,

div.head: Social Service League.
div.p: Social Service League.

- - Sir,—Evena person profoundly ignorant of ordinary newspaper controversy can readily see that Mr. Morton's letter is a sickly attempt to be "funny." It may be an easy was to escape a difficulty but it is not a very i creditable one, and s surely not a very laudable pro- cedure for the Secretary of a Social service League. I would beg to remind Mr. Morton that we are not play- ing at some child's game, but that we are striving to be men, endeavouring to act our part in the real game of life, and to do our best in the interests of humanity. If I wanted to ridicule him. I could do it, but I ask myself, is it worth it? What good can come of it? For a Society to wash it's dirty lineal in public is, I am sorry to say, a somewhat frequent occurrence. There may be plenty of fun in it for the onlookers but I have never yet known an occasion when it has proved to be profitable to either the Society or the individuals con- cerned. Mr. Morton reminds me that I " knew of the tension existing between himself and Mr. Dannico." But, Sir, because I knew that a tension existed between these two gentlemen it did not, in any way, interfere with my actions. I believe that no public work should be dragged at the heels of personal differences. We have only to look round us in many directions and we shall see I think, the public good being sacrificed to personal differences, and with what sorry results. I have already given what I believe to be a true account of the proceedings ands() far as lam personally concerned the matter is now ended.—Yonrs truly, EDMUND OSBORNE, Financial Secretary, Social Service League. Warrington, 9th No veraber, 1905.

-- Sir,—The "funny" reply of Mr. Morton in last week's issue carries with it its own refutation and further comment is unnecessa.ry,—Yours etc., HERBERT DIINNICO. (President of the Social Service League).

div.head: Liberals and Non-Traders,
div.p: Liberals and Non-Traders,

Sir,—l venture to take the liberty of concluding from the tone of your, shall I say, bold comment on the Liberal fiasco of November Ist, that you actually favour an alliance with the Non-Traders. Possibly your inten- tions do not go so far, but the idea is certainly suggested in your note. Whatever merit there may be, or may not be, in the idea, I think recent affairs have rendered it imperative that the Liberal Association should seriously recon- sider its position in view of the approaching general election. So far the line of action has, officially, been I unierstand, to shun like the plague both Traders and Non-Traders. But while thishas been the accepted policy it has not been carried out to the strict letter. Whether it was the fault of the Non-Traders, the Liberals, or both, the fact remains that on November Ist, the two were directly opposed, and the Liberals lost, The latter fought officially for Imperial politics and the rank and tile evidently voted for purity in municipal government. I have since heard that, to take Town Hall Ward as an instance, the majority of electors who went to the poll were Liberal, while the Tories largely abstained from voting. Clearly, therefore, many Liberals forsook the party colours for the time being and recorded their votes as they were influenced by the lesser, but more pressing, local reasons. The lesson it seems to me, and as you pointed out, is that it will not do for Liberals and Non-Traders to be antagonistic if the chances of the party at the General Election are to be furthered. There are, Mr. Editor, I more Liberal Non-Traders than is realised at the head- quarters in Bewsey-street. The fact that so many Non- Trading Councillors happen to be Conservative is nothing to go by. We might have had three Liberal councillors returned this November if we had had Liberal candidates honest enough, and determined enough, to avow their sympathy with non- trading principles. The policy of ignoring non-trading when it was the most potent factor in the elections is comparable to nothing so much as the ostrich burying its hea,cl in the sand and imagining that it is invisible to its enemies. As a Liberal who is keenly desirous of seeing a repe- tition this next election of the never-to-be-forgotten triumph of 1880, I write to demand that the unique chances of the party at the next election shall not be ruined by a stubborn determination on the part of its leaders to ignore palpable facts. As you have pointed out, Mr. Editor," with such an &eject as purity in Government all true Liberals mast be in sympathy." They are, and they do not see why their party should, to its own detriment, be at daggers drawn with the members of another party professing and wishing for this ideal. Let us face facts sir, and by a frank discussion endeavour to so shape the course of the Liberal ship that she will not be continually meeting snags which are not marked on the political chart. I am, sir, yours faithfully,
" ISSO."

[Oar correspondent, in his opening paragraph, draws an inference which we must repudiate. An " alliawse with the Non-Traders "was not what we suggested or had in mind. Probably it would suit neither Liberals nor Non-Traders, but we do think that the purity of Government both civic and national should be made a plank in the Liberal plat- form and not left as a monopoly for the Non- Traders. If a community of aims resulted in a unity of action, well and good.—ED. "E."l

Prenntation to Dr. Lunt, Lymm. On Friday evening last, Dr. Lunt, who is leaving Lyinin after a fourteen years residence in the district, I was made the recipient of a travelling case, with solid silver fittings, a large kit bag and a beautifully illuminated address, The address, which bore the signatures of the courraitteeresconsible for the arrang- ing of the presentation read : " We, the undersigned members of the committee representing over two ,hundred of your friends and patients, are earnestly desirous of expressing to you our appreciation of your -oenvices towards us during fourteen years' residence in Lymin. To all of as, rich and poor alike, you have endeared yourself by your unfailing help and sympathy as a physician and a public medical officer Your skill, your time and your best energies have always been placed ungrudgingly at our disposal. We therefore ask you to accept the accompanying token of our sincere gratitude and esteem, hoping it may serve to recall to your wind the many you leave in Lynam who, regretting your departure, heartily wish you and yours health mid happiness wherever the future may lead you. Dated this 3rd day of November 1905?' There are three small views on the address of " The Cross" " Lymm Church and the Dam "and " The Bongs." Mr. A. D. happily, some kind friends of his in Warrington had suggested that as his predecessors took a fairly active 1 part in the public affairs of the town so he might do worse than humbly try to follow in their footsteps, he might have been a victim to golf for the rest of his natural existence. (Laug.hter). It was very certain that if anyone took up politics seriously and was con- nected with business as well, like he was, he would not have a considerable amount of leisnre for golf. Speak- ing in a friendly way between themselves, he might say that although during his holidays in Switzerland he got a fair turn at golf, he was sorry to say in England those clubs of his week after week looked at him in the most reproachful manner as if to say "Why are you not doing your duty ?" (Laughter.) Then music, with which their good friend Mr. R. B. Pearson was so closely associated and did so much to popularize and raise in tone in Warrington, did not get as good a share of prac- tice as he would like to give to it. He was happy to say that other members of the family did their duty, and if they cared to have his sister play occasionally there—(applause)--he could assure them it would give her the greatest pleasure, because she ' only told him so the other day. Mr. Croslield congratu- lated Mr. E. A. Sanders upon the excellence of the programme and expressed great gratification that the , gathering was graced with the prosence of so many ladies. Speaking frankly and politically the attend- ance reminded one of

THE SPLENDID PROGRESS which the ladies of Warrington had made in political ' activity during the last twelve months. (Hear, hear.) The Women's Liberal Association had grown to propor- tions which meant an enormous influence on the political development of the town. (Applause.) In apologising for having to leave the concert early, Mr. Orosfield explained that he had to do a great deal of work at Hoylake before Friday afternoon when, in response to the courteous invitation of Sir David Gamble, he was going to St. Helens to meet young Winston Churchill. (Applause and a Voice "Bring him here.") That was just what he was going to try and do. (Applause.) He might say they had been in corres- pondence with Mr. Churchill for some months and he (Mr. Crosfleld) did not suppose there was any man lathe kingdom who was more sought after at the moment as a publics speaker on either side than Mr. Churchill, because he knew how to hit out straight from the shoulder and anything more complete and conclusive than his exposure of the nonsense that emanated from Birmingham he (Mr. Crosfield) hai never read or listened to. (Applause.) Mr. Churchill had suggested perhaps he could help them in Warrington if he came down here and

ADDRESSED A MEETING IN THE PARR HALL on the eve of the opening of Parliament. (Applause.) He was sure all present would agree that if he (Mr. Crosfield) could only just clinch the nail and on Friday persuade Mr. Churchill to come, he would have done a great deal better service than by any attempt to make a speech on political affairs that night. There was only one subject, as regarded politics, that he would like to mention. He continually heard it said "we are sick of this fiscal question." Well there was not the slightest eoubt that a great many people were sick of it, and there was such a division of opinion amongst the people who spread that precious gospel that he thought they would b 3 even more sick of it before they had carried the fight very much further. (Applause). So far as they were con- cerned as Liberals they were not at all sick of the fiscal question. He did not mean only that it was a great help to them as a party, that it was bringing all the Progressive ranks together in a solid phalanx which would not be broken by any man in imperial circles or local circles unless he incurred the very gravest respon• sibility. (Hear, hear). The question was focussing opinion for them in a way that was of great advantage to the progressive forces of the country. (Applause). Therefore they were not sick of it at all as a party measure. They were not sick of it for another reason. They held that, though they were party men and were fighting as party men, at the same time there was something more behind Liberal politics than that, and anyone who looked back on the work which Cobden, Bright and Gladstone had done was going to think twice before he allowed any American party "boss," or political plunger,to upset the finances and the trade of the whole of the country, to

DAMAGE THE WHOLE OF THE COUNTRY and above all to attack Lancashire itself. (Applause,) He hoped however sick the authors of that precious programme might become, they as Liberals would not loose their tenacious grip of the great principles which their fathers fought for and which they of the present generation had got to tight for. They had heard of all our trades, first one trade then the other, going down. (Laughter.) He was not going to run through the whole category but he would ask them to look at the threatened woollen trade, which was supposed to be one of the worst. It was now in a prosperous con- dition with excellent prospects before it. (Applause.) Then let them look at the poor tin plate trade which of all others was going to "pot." (Laughter and applause.) Why, that was smiling too. (Applause.) Then again let them come to

THE GREAT TRADE OF LANCASILTRE on which millions of people in this country depended for a healthy livelihood—the cotton industry. They were told by the wonderful prophet that cotton would go too. The exports of cotton—although they as Free Traders did not take exportation as the sole measure of the condition of British trade, because the home market was most important—but taking Mr. I Chamberlain on his own ground, they could tell him that the exports of cotton in the llrst nine months of this year were fourteen million sterling ahead of what they were in the first nine months of last year. (Applause.) Those were facts which they were not going to get sick of, and they were going to keep them well in mind. They were also going to keep well in mind the record which they had to look back upon—the frightful expenditure,the frightful waste, with both hands, out of capital, the squandering of thirty or forty years' savings of the best English statesmanship, the frightful delusion and lies which were circulated in the nation and led us into that disastrous war and the conclusion of it—that pernicious and evil importation of slavery or semi-slavery, call it whichever they liked in the dominions of the Crown. Those were things which they would not forget. (Applause.). He was sure

EVERY TRADE UNIONIST in Warrington would keep his eye on judge made law. (Hear, hear.) He spoke as an employer of labour, but he was certain,—and all history proved it—that we were less in danger of strikes and that there was a better chance of employers and employees coming to an agree- ment if they had large and properly supported organiza- tions of labour just as they had organizations of capital. (Applause.) He believed that the present state of trade union law was a matter which appealed to every trade unionist in Warrington, whatever his shade of politics might be on other questions. Although he (Mr. Cros- fleld)had not exhausted more than a quarter of the work that lay before them, he could say that they were not at all sick of their programme. Whatever might be the feelings of those misguided and unfortunate friends of theirs,—because he had many Tory friends in Warrington, and he spoke ill personally of no-one, but only of principles—they as Libera.'s were strong in their creed and in their programme, even if the Tories might feel a little bit unhappy at the prospect before them. He would give their Conservative friends a word of comfort. Don't let them be down-hearted—(laughter)— but let them recognize that it was not only for the Liberals, but it would be a jolly good thing for them if there was a little change in the administration— (hear, bear)—and if the Liberals could put our Imperial Government on a sounder basis so that they would get better value for their money, more efficiency and less clap-trap. (Applause).

Stockton Heath Rugby Unionists gained a wel earned victory over Sale " A " by 11 points to nil' W. Gibbs at full back, although hardly playing up to the previous Saturday's form was quite safe and kicked ! with great judgement. Of the threequarters V 7. Bouchier and A. V. Ferguson did c 0111.9 really good work and the line as a whole played well H. Daven- port and A. Bradshaw at half played a sound game, although Bradshaw shows a tendency to stick to the ball too long. The forwards completely overran their opponents and the three tries scored by Daintith were all obtained through good work by the forwards in the loose. One or two of the forwards were guilty of kicking the ball back into the scrum and, preventing the backs getting going. Had they heeled smartly instead the score would undoubtedly have been greater. J. Daintith in the loose wtls the pick of the forwards and Gibbs, Cook and Barker did excellent work in the scrtuns. The Sale backs, behind a beaten pack did good work repeatedly breaking up rushes by the home forwards and tackling with determination.

div.head: Rugby Football.
div.p: Rugby Football.
[By " Ovalist."l

There was a very close struggle between Warring- ton and Runcorn on Saturday and eventually victory rested with the Linnets. The fact that the homesters could only just get the better of Warrington's depleted forces is a fairly convineing proof that they are not quite so strong a team as their record would suggest. Only one defeat in eight matches is something like championship form, but Runcorn are far from being a champion fifteen. They were no better than Warring- ton an Saturday, and if the Cup-holders had had any- thing like the team of last April I think they would have made mince meat of the Cheshire men, good as their defensive powers are. There is little doubt in my mind that when once the Runcorn men begin to leave their own peculiar pitch they will lose points rapidly.

On Saturday Warrington put one of the most dis- organised teams in the field that has ever been their ill-fortune to muster. In my experience they were never before absolutely without s wing-threequarter, which was the state of things at Runcorn. The two men who did duty were Knight, full-back, and Brooks, half-back,and they Are very nearly the best men in the line, All Warrington's strength was for- ward, but it did not suffice to secure points, though much of the game was spent in the Runcorn half. The men behind had neither speed nor combination—the first-named was the most needed—and try..getting appeared next to impossible. Yet the vititors should have wou, or at least halved the points.

At the interval they were leading by a goal to nil and having the best of the game. Runcorn looked no more likely to score than did Warrington until the latter threw all their advantage away by bad management. I have already indicated that the best part of the Warringtoa team was the forward division and yet when Runcorn got dangerous for the first time, the forwards were weakened by the withdrawal of Thomas to assist the threequarters. As a result the eight Runcorn forwards beat the seven Warrington ' men for possession six times in succession within ten yards of the line and,of course, they eventually scored. All this time Thomas was a looker-on, whereas in the pack he could have made just enough difference to have swept the Runcorn pack of its feet and prevented a score. The same idiotic thing happened again near the end of the game. Runcorn were practically given possession near the line and Jolly dropped a goal. I felt sufficiently disgusted almost to vow not to watch the Warrington men until they learned common sense. I defy anybody to point to a single instance this season when Thomas's transference to the threequarter line has not been Warrington's loss. They would have won at Halifax but for the same silly policy and they would have won at Runcorn on Saturday. Even the Runcorn men on the stand could see .the crass stupidity of Warrington in handing over their undoubted superiority forward to their opponents at the most critical part of the game.

The game itself was an exceedingly poor one from the standpoint of attractiveness. The homo halves punted to touch persistently and Warrington were little better in this respect. Jolley was the worst sinner, and if it is one way of winning when his team has the lead, it will soon lose Runcorn the name they once had of playing attractive football. Their work generally was full of vigour and determination and whatever else can be said it cannot be gainsaid that the Linnets have well-earned their splendid defensive record. They have only had their line crossed three times compared with Warrington's twelve. Harrison made an excellent substitute for Houghton at back, while Butterworth and young Allen late of Warrington were the pick of the threequarters.

Warrington were poor outside the scrummage. The halves were both short of enterprise and smartness, Hockenhall being the inferior man of the two. He is showing not a glimpse of the form which gained him County honours last season and appears to me to have gone stale. Thomas played a great game ala Gallaher and very much incensed the Runcorn crowd, but he would be better in the pack. Brooks would have been more use in the centre. Hewitt did some good saving, but he is slow and does not know yet how to time his passes. Knight's kicking was of good service and he was. twice very near to scoring a try. The referee was the gentleman who officiated at Warrington's two home defeats last season, and he was objected to by the Warrington men. I don't think they will have any better opinion of him after Saturday's match.

Leeds and Keighley now share the leadership of the League with Oldham occupying third, but a relatively stronger position. The success of Keighley is even more surprising than that of Runcorn, and seven victories out of eight matches does not point to second division form by any means.

Warrington should easily obtain two League points to-day at the expense of Rochdale Hornets, whom they defeated in the first round of the Lancashire Cup. The Hornets have since been strengthened by the inclusion of Baxter, Blincow, and a couple of for- wards, but Warrington ought to find in them easy victims for all that. At Rochdale, where Warrington were no better represented than now, the score was 10 points to nil in their favour, and should have been double.
The team has been selected as follows : Hallam, full back ; Harris, Brooks, Isherwood, and Knight, three-quarters ; Boardman, Preston, Thomas, Shugars, Belton, Cook, llarmer and Swift, forwards.

Last Saturday the "A" team persued the even tenour of their way at the expense of Runcorn the score again leaching the twenties. To-day they will have a stiffer ordeal at Rochdale, but I quite expect they will emerge triumphant. Their selected twelve are : C. Ashton, full back; Kenyon, Jordan, Hewitt Ind Lloyd threequarters ; Hall and Garside, halves; Ernest Lunt, Heath, Hartley, Fairhurst and W. Ashton, forwards.

Even Dai. Davies at Huddersfield has not escaped the Warrington epidemic of damaged shoulders. Playing against Wakefield Trinity on Saturday he Unstained a dislocation of the shoulder which*will keep him out of the team for some weeks.

I hear that there is now much greater probability of Warrington securing the transfer of a well-known left wing threequarter than there was a few weeks ago. That the deal will soon be completed is the general and ardent hope in the town.

div.head: Hockey.
div.p: Hockey.

Latchford met Stockton Eleath at Latchford on Saturday last, the second elevens playing at Warrington. Both Stockton Heath teams were tipped to win, but alas! prophets and critics were alike confounded, and both teams lost. Perhaps it is hardly wise to say much at present, as the teams meet again in their return games on the 18th inst., but still Latchford won by four goals to one.

The home team at Latchford had their opponents beaten almost from the commencement. They proved to be in fine form and playing a capital combined game they thaintaioed a vigorous attack and defence with which the visitors failed to cope. There were, of course, plenty of exciting moments when the Stockton Heath forwards invaded the home circle, but the final attempt was usually frustrated by the home defence, or was spoiled by off-side play. Soon after the game started Spensley put in a terrific shot which, however, was too high by inches. This was improved upon later when Knight scored with a good shot. He soon after- wards added to this and before half-time was called Cliffe beat the visitors' opposition and running through on his own scored again. This proved to be all the scoring up to half-time, the score then reading Latch- ford three, Stockton Heath nil.

The second half opened in a rather sensational manner as from the bully off the visitors forwards broke away, beat the opposing backs, and Banks scored. Then it was thought they were going to show what we have been led to believe was their true form, but they flattered only to deceive. Ido not mean by this that they fell away, but they did not improve, and though from time to time they took up the attack, they were unable to add the finishing touch and for the most part wereion the defensive. Latchford forwards again invaded the visitors circle, and Knight scored his third goal. Then the result was placed beyond all doubt. In fact Latchford might have further added to their score, as with an absolutely open goal mouth in front of him, Cotton in his excitement, shot rather wildly, and only miEsed the post apparently by a hair's breadth. Nothing further however was added, and Latchford therefore won as above stated by 4 goals to

'the chief feature of the game was Latchford's untiring efforts. This along with the excellent combination which they undoubtedly showed, seemed to rather upset the calculations of the visitors, who came on the field full of confidence,and their play suffered in consequence. Whilst therefore Latchford excelled the mselves,Stockton Heath proved to be off their form, at least the form we have been led to expect from theta, the home team thoroughly deserved their win.

There has been rather an unfortunate and regrettable sequel to the game. Someone connected with the Stockton Heath Club I believe, has been indiscreet enough (to say the least of it) to report the match to the contri- butors of " Hockey Notes to the " Daily Mail " and "Daily Despatph." These reportsare far from flattering and in fact art' a direct insult to the referees concerned. The game is compared to a football match in the "Daily Mail "and the report says that a great deal of "body play " took place, and advises the Stockton Heath Club to bring in some outside referee to control the game. The" Daily Despatch" report says," the game degener- ated into a scrimmage.' My object in mentioning this is to give them an emphatic denial from the com- mittee of the Latchford Club. The game was not by any means rough, especially taking into consideration the local element in the game, no more body play than is usual with the best of teams, county teams included was used, and Stockton Heath transgressed in this direction as much or perhaps more than Latchford. and the game did not by any means degenerate into a scrimmage. This is not simply a Latchford club's account, but is the independent testimony of independ- ent persons. Such a report as that in the " Daily Mail "is calculated to damage the reputation of the Latchford Club, and It is a pity that whoever gave it to Mr. Fletcher could not take the beating with better sportsmanship and give to Latchford a little of the credit they undoubtedly deserve.
Stockton Heath 2nd v. Latchfor,4 2nd played at War- rington on Saturday as indicated above, and the match resulted in a win for Latchford by 1 goal to nil.

I Early on the visitors scored, Albinson going through on his own,and recording a capital goal. Unfortunately 'Warburton had to retire when the game had only been in progress a few minutes, as he got rather a nasty knock on the knee, leaving Latchford with only ten men for the rest of the game. Even so, they held the upper band, particularly in the first half. Their defence proved too much for the home forwards, and although the latter had three corners just previous to time being called, they were unable to break through.

div.head: " THE GEMS."
div.p: " THE GEMS."
Pleasing Entertainments at the Parr Hall.

It is difficult to account for the smallness of the attendances at the entertainments given in the Parr Hall on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings by a versatile company known as "The Gems." The programmes submitted were exceedingly interesting and the attrac- tion certainly merited a much greater share of public patronage. Those townspeople who did attend were warm in their appreciation, the various items pleasing not less by the brightness and originality that characterized many of them than by the highly creditable way in which all were given. The company has an extensive repertoire of songs, duets, trios, quartettes, quintettes, operettas, and sketches and the selections made were admirable. The artistes comprising "The Gems " are Miss Elsie Jones (soprano), Miss Olive Mortimer (contralto), Mr. Edgar Stevens (baritone), Mr. Wallace Kennedy (tenor), Mr. Kenna Lawson (humorist) and Mr. Harold Scott (solo pianist. and accompanist). To deal only with Tuesday's programme, the company figured to advantage in several laughable items, one of the best being descriptive of the excitements of a motor car journey with its inevitable break down. Miss Elsie Jones elicited a full measure of praise for piquant renderings of A painted butterfly " and " buy my lavender" while Miss Olive Mortimer's rich contralto voice found full scope in" Out on the rocks," "We too "and "The banks of Allan water," which were expressively interpreted. Mr. Wallace Kennedy gave a pleasing little song "Just my sweetheart "in meritorious !style. Mr. Edgar Stevens, who possesses a robust baritone voice, delighted the audience with "The tramp " and " Queen of C trolina " which he sang with fine spirit. Mr. Stevens is also an exceptionally clever dancer and this accomplishment considerably enhanced the pleasure of his performance of the latter item. Responding to an encore he gave "An old garden" very feelingly. Mr. Kenna Lawson was responsible for several humorous songs and sketches which kept the house in continual merriment, his original illustrations of " style" being particularly good. Mr. Harold Scott accompanied very tastefully and his brilliantly-executed solo " Rhapsody II" (Liszt) was well,received. On Wednesday there was a change of programme and the company again provided a delightful entertainment which gave the utmost satisfaction.

div.head: Sad Burning Fatality.
div.p: Sad Burning Fatality.

The death occurred on Saturday under sad circum- stances of Miss Amy Payton, aged 23. daughter of Mr. James Payton, of the Blue Back Inn, Allen-street. At the inquest which was conducted at the Police Station on Monday by Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, Mr. Payton stated that at 8.10 on Saturday evening, the 28th ult. deceased wont,upstairs .Shortly afterwards he heard a noise on the bedroom floor an he and others went upstairs awl found deceased on the landing with her clothing on lire The flames were extinguished and Dr. Adams was sent for and ordered deceased's removal to the Infirmary. Deceased had for fourteen years suffered from fits and he was of opinion that she was seized with a bout and sot tire to her clothing with a taper she was carrying—lt appeared that deceased made a statement to that effect on being admitted to the Infir- mary—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death " and expressed their deep sympathy with Mr. Payton. The Coroner said he had heard of the great care which Mr. Payton had taken of his daughter and of the great love and affection he had shown towards her.

div.head: WARRINGTON MAN IN CANADA.
div.p: A WARRINGTON MAN IN CANADA.

Mr. F. J. Lord has forwarded to us the following letter which he has received from Mr. P. Taylor, form- erly an employee in the joinery department of Messrs Crosflelds'. The writer was first violin in Crosfields' Works Orchestra, and it would appear still finds time for his hobby in spite of the many cares of a hard colonial life.

div.head: Virden, Manitoba,
div.p: Virden, Manitoba,

Canada. Dear Sir,—As you would no doubt like to know how lam gAtting on in the new country I take this oppor- tunity of writing to you. Well, sir, lam now settled on my own farm of 1-60 acres. I bought the same for 2,000 dollars from the Mayor of Virden, Mr. Langtry, Canadian. It is certainly a very pretty place. The land is somewhat rolling, but the soil is excellent. I have now gone through my first season, having plowed, sown, reaped and thrashed 75 acres of wheat, oats and barley. The results are 500 bushels of wheat, 440 of oats and 130 of barley. I have a good mare and a very good foal, a very fair team, 3 cows and 4 calves, and I have had a very good result from my garden. Then too we have half-a-dozen pigs, about 50 hens and some chicks, so you see we have plenty of company. I am trying to get together a string band. The difficulty when we get it together will be to find a name for it. There is an undoubted market here the growth of which is an assured thing. Indeed it is my firm belief that the North West Territory will before very long be one of the best markets—it is now growing very quickly, and I should like to see the old firm casting its nets here. I hope you have had a good time with your musical endeavours of late. I should be pleased to hear from you and to know the result of the year's work.—Hoping, B:c., Yours truly,
P. TAYLOR.

A special meeting of the Town Council will be held, this (Friday) evening at 6 o'clock in deference to a requisition from five of the seven members of the Investigation Committee appointed to consider the charges brought against two members of the Town, Council under the Corrupt Practices Act. It will be remembered that at the two previous monthly meetings of the Town Council a strong endeavour was made to secure that the statement of the case to go before the Attorney-General should be laid before the Investigation Committee. This w/is refused by the Town Clerk, and at the meeting on October 31st last, the resolutions of Councillor Lord bearing upon the matter were ruled out of order.
The notice calling to-night's meeting reads as follows :

Town Clerk's Office, Town Hall, 6th November, 1905. Sir,—ln pursuance of the following requisition Warrington, November 2nd, 1905. "To the Mayor of Warrington, Alderman Bolton, J.P. We, tho undersigned, five members of the War- rington Town Council, do hereby request you to call a meeting of the Town Council.
B i :less : To consider the proceedings of the late Investi- gation Committee, and the proceedings of the Council in relation thereto, and to propose resolu- tions thereon."

(Signed) William Pierpoint. Fred Stott. Jas. G. Craik. John Lord. Thomas H. Ashroft. the Mayor requests your attendance at a Meeting of the Council of this Borough, to be holden in the Council Chamber, on Friday nsxt, the 10th day of November, 1905, at Six o'clock in the evening, as a Special Meeting of the Council, to take into consideration and determine upon the business set out in the said Requisition. J. LYON WHITTLE, Town Clerk.

We understand that a resolution will be proposed to-night with the idea of testing the feeling of the Council on the point as to whether the statement of the case should have been laid before the Investigation Committee prior to being sent to the Attorney-General,

It is now extensively used in many countries, and everywhere acknowledged as the Best Tonic Remedy known.

Quinine and the active principles of the following well-known herbs : Sarsaparilla, Saffron, Gentian, Lavender, Burdock, and Dandelion, scientifically pre- pared, and in such happy proportions as to form a Tonic Bitters positively unequalled.
3. What is its action?

It assists and promotes Digestion strengthens the Nerves and Muscles, purifies the Blood enlivens the Spirits, and removes all Obstructions and Impurities in the Human Body. It gives tone to the whole system. It strengthens and fortifies those parts which have been weakened by Disease, and are consequently more liable to Colds and unhealthful influences. It has gained the Highest Recommendations as the Best Family Medicin e and a remedy for every kind of Weakness.
4. What Diseases is it specidty recommeitela for;?

Influenza, and the after effects of an attack of Influenza, Indigestion, Chest Affections and Diseases of the Liver in all their various forms, Neuralgia and all Nervous Disorders, Depression of Spirits, General Weakness, Loss of Appetite, Sleeplessness.

using it?
No ; the working man need not abstain from his labour, the mother from her houThold duties, or the child be kept from school while using it.

MARY MUSTY, , a cook at Woodham House,Wrough- • ton, near Swindon, says : Three years ago I suffered acutely from indigestion and biliousness. My appetite left me, I had no relish for food, I couldn't sleep at night, I was frequently sick, and had some terrible headaches. So reduced did I become that I seemed to lose all use in my limbs. At times I would be as helpless as a baby' and just drop_down anywhere and faint. "Two doctors attended me, but did me no good. I couldn't digest food, and was reduced almost to a shadow. I was taken to the Swindon Hospital and treated for DEBILITY but got worse, and only remained a fortnight. I was next taken away for a change of air, but got worse. Reading about Bile Beans, I decided to try them. After finishing the first box I could take a little food, while my sickness was not so bad, and I didn't faint so often. I can now say that after I had taken eight boxes of Bile Beans I found myself again completely restored to health." - , , , , . ,

and judgment. Lamb often passed for something in between an imbecile, a brute or a buffoon, and one could only regret the lack of appreciation of these who regarded him in that light Lanai) did not care twopence for the feelings of anyone when be was in the mood for writing. Throughout his essays we had a subtle and delicate play of fancy, wit and humour. Lamb's imagination was not of the ethereal order. It winged a lowly flight and yet was effective. There was very little of the purely ideal element in his wok for he dealt with experience of life and of books and in his service memory was a willing slave. Lamb revived a true appreciation of Shakespeare and introduced the Elizabethan to the people of his day. We liked him because he was so human, so frail and so much like ourselves. The lecturer concluded by saying he was sure after his hearers had read Lamb's works they would agree that of all the writer's in the English language Lamb was the one who would claim their affections and their hearts.
